# Actor Kit: the full documentation

Generated from https://actorkit.dev (index: https://actorkit.dev/llms.txt).

# Overview

Source: https://actorkit.dev/getting-started/overview/

## When to use Actor Kit

Actor Kit is for applications where **multiple users interact with shared, real-time state**. Each piece of shared state is an actor — a Durable Object that processes messages one at a time and pushes updates to connected clients.

Good fits:
- Collaborative apps (shared documents, whiteboards, project boards)
- Multiplayer games (zones, lobbies, match state)
- Real-time dashboards (live metrics, monitoring)
- Chat and messaging (rooms, threads, presence)
- Auction/bidding systems (competitive real-time updates)

Not a good fit:
- Static sites or CRUD apps without real-time requirements
- Batch processing or data pipelines
- Applications that don't need WebSocket connections

## Key terms

- **Actor** — a Durable Object instance with state, roles, messages, and views
- **Message** — a named action sent to the actor. On the server, defined in the `messages` block. On the client, sent as `{ type: "INCREMENT", amount: 5 }`
- **View** — a role-scoped projection of the actor's state, sent to connected clients
- **Role** — a predicate that determines what a caller can see and do
- **Lifecycle** — `connect` and `disconnect` handlers that fire on WebSocket open/close
- **Guard** — a predicate on a message that checks authorization or preconditions before the handler runs
- **Contract** — the typed object returned by `kit.actor()` (the kit comes from `setup()`), from which clients, tests, and refs derive types

## How it works

```
Browser → WebSocket → CF Worker → Durable Object (Actor)
                                    ├── State (SQLite)
                                    ├── Roles (who can do what)
                                    ├── Messages (what changes state)
                                    └── Views (what each role sees)
```

1. A Worker authenticates the caller and routes the request to the right Durable Object
2. The DO reads the caller identity from headers and resolves the caller's role
3. Messages from the client are validated (Zod) and routed to the role's handler
4. State changes are persisted to SQLite and broadcast as view updates
5. Each connected client gets a role-specific projection of the state

## How it compares

| | Actor Kit | PartyKit | Liveblocks | Socket.IO |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Programming model | Message-driven (typed messages) | Imperative | Document mutations | Imperative |
| Runtime | CF Durable Objects | CF Durable Objects | Managed cloud | Self-hosted |
| State model | Actor per entity | Room per party | Document per room | No built-in state |
| State changes | Typed messages → pure handlers | Arbitrary mutations | CRDT operations | Arbitrary emissions |
| Authorization | Role-based, derived from state | Custom middleware | Custom middleware | Custom middleware |
| Sync protocol | Binary delta or JSON | JSON | CRDT | JSON |
| Persistence | Automatic (DO SQLite) | Manual | Managed | Manual |
| TypeScript | Full inference from contract | Partial | SDK types | Partial |

## Architecture

Actor Kit embraces Cloudflare's infrastructure:

| CF Feature | How Actor Kit uses it |
|------------|----------------------|
| Durable Objects | Each actor is a DO — single-threaded, globally addressable |
| DO SQLite | State persistence, transactional outbox |
| DO Alarms | Durable timers that survive hibernation |
| DO WebSocket Hibernation | Caller metadata stored as tags, survives restarts |
| Workers | Route requests, serve UI, stamp caller identity |

## Next steps

- [Installation](https://actorkit.dev/getting-started/installation/) — set up your project
- [Quick Start](https://actorkit.dev/getting-started/quick-start/) — build a counter in 5 minutes
- [Counter Guide](https://actorkit.dev/examples/counter/) — full walkthrough with UI

# Installation

Source: https://actorkit.dev/getting-started/installation/

## Install

Server (Cloudflare Worker):

```bash
pnpm add @actor-kit/core @actor-kit/worker zod
```

Client (browser):

```bash
pnpm add @actor-kit/core @actor-kit/client
```

| Package | Usage |
|---------|-------|
| `@actor-kit/core` | Shared: `schema`, `view`, type primitives (`uint32`, `string`, etc.), `encode`, `decode` |
| `@actor-kit/worker` | Server: `setup` (the kit, with `kit.actor`), `createActorClass`, `withCallerIdentity` |
| `@actor-kit/client` | Browser: `actorClient` — WebSocket connection with binary decoding |
| `@actor-kit/react` | React: `actorContext` — hooks for view, send, role |
| `@actor-kit/test` | Testing: `testActor` — fast unit tests without Wrangler |

Actor Kit uses [Zod](https://zod.dev) for message payload validation at runtime boundaries.

## Prerequisites

- [Cloudflare Workers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/) account
- [Wrangler](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/wrangler/) CLI (`pnpm add -D wrangler`)
- Node.js 20+
- pnpm (recommended)

## Project Setup

### 1. Create a Worker project

```bash
pnpm create cloudflare@latest my-actor-app
cd my-actor-app
pnpm add @actor-kit/core @actor-kit/worker zod
```

### 2. Configure wrangler.toml

```toml
name = "my-actor-app"
main = "src/worker.ts"
compatibility_date = "2024-09-25"
compatibility_flags = ["enable_ctx_exports"]

[[durable_objects.bindings]]
name = "MY_ACTOR"
class_name = "MyActor"

[[migrations]]
tag = "v1"
new_sqlite_classes = ["MyActor"]
```

Key points:
- `enable_ctx_exports` enables automatic actor discovery via `ctx.exports` (recommended for single-Worker deployments)
- `new_sqlite_classes` enables DO SQLite storage for your actor

### 3. Define your actor

See the [Quick Start](https://actorkit.dev/getting-started/quick-start/) for a complete example.

## TypeScript

Actor Kit is written in TypeScript with strict mode. Types are inferred from your actor definition — annotate the state type once on each handler, and the kit types the rest. `kit.actor()` returns a typed contract that preserves all generic information for downstream consumers.

Wrangler generates Worker types for you — no manual type package needed:

```bash
pnpm wrangler types
```

This creates a `worker-configuration.d.ts` file with types for your bindings and the CF runtime. Re-run it whenever you change `wrangler.toml`.

## Testing

`@actor-kit/test` provides `testActor()` — a typed test harness that runs your actor without a Cloudflare runtime:

```bash
pnpm add -D @actor-kit/test vitest
```

```typescript
import { testActor } from "@actor-kit/test";
import { CounterContract } from "./counter.contract";

const t = testActor(CounterContract);
const state = t.init({});
const next = await t.send(state, "alice", { type: "INCREMENT" });
// next.count === 1 — fully typed from the contract
```

`testActor()` covers role evaluation, message routing, Zod validation, guards, view projection, and emission capture. See [Testing](https://actorkit.dev/concepts/testing/) for the full guide.

## For AI coding agents

The docs come in agent-friendly forms: [llms.txt](https://actorkit.dev/llms.txt) indexes every page,
[llms-full.txt](https://actorkit.dev/llms-full.txt) holds them all in one file, and every package ships the
pages its users need in its `docs/` folder (`node_modules/@actor-kit/worker/docs/`), matching the installed
version. Errors and refusals carry a `code` whose page is under [/errors/](https://actorkit.dev/errors/).

# Quick Start

Source: https://actorkit.dev/getting-started/quick-start/

Build a shared counter that multiple users can increment in real-time. The full source is in [`examples/counter/`](https://github.com/actor-kit/actor-kit/tree/main/examples/counter).

## 1. Define the Contract

The contract lives in its own file. It defines state, messages, roles, and views — everything both server and client need to know about the actor:

```typescript
// src/counter.contract.ts
import { z } from "zod";
import { schema, view, uint32, string } from "@actor-kit/core";
import { setup } from "@actor-kit/worker";

type CounterState = { count: number; lastUpdatedBy: string };

const CounterView = schema({ count: uint32, lastUpdatedBy: string });

// The kit: what the actor declares up front (events, states, env). A counter declares none.
const counter = setup({});

export const CounterContract = counter.actor("counter", {
  input: z.object({}),
  init: (): CounterState => ({ count: 0, lastUpdatedBy: "" }),

  roles: {
    user: () => true,
  },

  messages: {
    INCREMENT: counter.message(z.object({}), (state: CounterState, _payload, { caller }) => ({
      ...state,
      count: state.count + 1,
      lastUpdatedBy: caller,
    })),
    DECREMENT: counter.message(z.object({}), (state: CounterState, _payload, { caller }) => ({
      ...state,
      count: Math.max(0, state.count - 1),
      lastUpdatedBy: caller,
    })),
  },

  views: {
    user: view.shared(CounterView, (state: CounterState) => ({
      count: state.count,
      lastUpdatedBy: state.lastUpdatedBy,
    })),
  },
});
export type CounterContract = typeof CounterContract;
```

Then the server file imports the contract value and creates the Durable Object class:

```typescript
// src/counter.server.ts
import { createActorClass } from "@actor-kit/worker";
import { CounterContract } from "./counter.contract";

export const Counter = createActorClass(CounterContract);
```

Key things happening:
- **`setup()`** returns the kit: it holds what the actor declares up front (events, states, env — all optional) and the helpers typed by them
- **`counter.actor()`** returns a typed contract — not a DO class. Everything derives from it.
- **`createActorClass()`** converts the contract into a Durable Object class
- **`counter.message()`** pairs a Zod schema with a handler — payload is validated before the handler runs. Annotate the state type once, on the handler's first parameter; the payload and `ctx` are typed for you
- **Messages are flat** — no nesting by role. Guards handle authorization (see [Todo List](https://actorkit.dev/examples/todo-list/))
- **Handlers are synchronous** — they return new state, no `async`/`await`
- **`schema()`** defines the view shape for binary encoding and TypeScript inference
- **The contract file is separate** — server imports the value, client imports only the type (see below)

## 2. Create the Worker

The Worker is the auth boundary. It authenticates the caller and stamps verified identity onto the request. The DO trusts the Worker.

```typescript
// src/worker.ts
import { withCallerIdentity } from "@actor-kit/worker";
import { Counter } from "./counter.server";

export { Counter };

interface Env {
  COUNTER: DurableObjectNamespace;
}

export default {
  async fetch(request: Request, env: Env): Promise<Response> {
    const url = new URL(request.url);

    // Route WebSocket connections to the Counter DO
    if (url.pathname.startsWith("/api/counter/")) {
      const actorId = url.pathname.split("/")[3] ?? "default";

      // Authenticate via session cookie.
      // PRODUCTION: validate a signed session cookie, OAuth token, or similar credential.
      const { callerId } = resolveCaller(request);

      const id = env.COUNTER.idFromName(actorId);
      const stub = env.COUNTER.get(id);

      // Spawn idempotently
      await stub.spawn({ actorId, caller: "system", callerType: "service", input: {} });

      // Stamp verified identity and forward to DO
      const stamped = withCallerIdentity(request, { callerId, callerType: "user" });
      return stub.fetch(stamped);
    }

    return new Response("Not found", { status: 404 });
  },
};

function resolveCaller(request: Request): { callerId: string } {
  const cookieHeader = request.headers.get("Cookie") ?? "";
  const match = cookieHeader.match(/(?:^|;\s*)caller_id=([^;]+)/);
  if (match?.[1]) return { callerId: decodeURIComponent(match[1]) };
  return { callerId: `user-${crypto.randomUUID().slice(0, 8)}` };
}
```

Key things happening:
- **`withCallerIdentity()`** scrubs any inbound identity headers, then stamps verified `callerId` and `callerType`
- **Cookie-based auth** — caller identity comes from a session cookie sent automatically by the browser. Never from URL query params.

## 3. Connect from the Browser

### Vanilla TypeScript

Client code uses `import type` to import the contract — this keeps Zod, handlers, and Cloudflare dependencies out of the browser bundle:

```typescript
import { actorClient } from "@actor-kit/client";
import type { CounterContract } from "./counter.contract";

// Type-only — no runtime contract value in the bundle
const CounterClient = actorClient<CounterContract>();

// Create a runtime connection — the browser sends the session cookie automatically.
// `path` (not `url`) means "relative to the current host". `host` is optional for
// overriding (e.g. in native apps).
const client = CounterClient.create({
  path: `/api/counter/my-counter`,
  initialView: { count: 0, lastUpdatedBy: "" }, // or an SSR snapshot
});
client.connect();

// Subscribe to typed views — binary delta decoding is handled transparently
client.subscribe((view) => {
  // view is typed: { count: number; lastUpdatedBy: string }
  console.log("Count:", view.count);
});

// Send typed messages — inferred from contract
client.send({ type: "INCREMENT" });
```

### React

The server loader fetches the initial snapshot from the DO. `useClient()` creates the client once and manages connect/disconnect on mount:

```tsx
import { actorContext } from "@actor-kit/react";
import type { CounterContract } from "./counter.contract";

const CounterCtx = actorContext<typeof CounterContract>();

// Server loader fetches the initial snapshot from the DO
export async function loader({ env, params, callerId }: { env: Env; params: { counterId: string }; callerId: string }) {
  const stub = env.COUNTER.get(env.COUNTER.idFromName(params.counterId));
  await stub.spawn({ actorId: params.counterId, caller: "system", callerType: "service", input: {} });
  const { snapshot } = await stub.getSnapshot(callerId, "user");
  return { counterId: params.counterId, snapshot };
}

function App({ counterId, snapshot }: { counterId: string; snapshot: { count: number; lastUpdatedBy: string } }) {
  // useClient creates the client once and manages connect/disconnect on mount.
  // initialView seeds useView() before the socket opens — no undefined state.
  // Cookies supply auth automatically.
  const client = CounterCtx.useClient({
    path: `/api/counter/${counterId}`,
    initialView: { role: "user", ...snapshot },
  });

  return (
    <CounterCtx.Provider client={client}>
      <Counter />
    </CounterCtx.Provider>
  );
}

function Counter() {
  const view = CounterCtx.useView();   // always defined — never undefined
  const send = CounterCtx.useSend();

  return (
    <div>
      <span>{view.count}</span>
      <button onClick={() => send({ type: "INCREMENT" })}>+</button>
      <button onClick={() => send({ type: "DECREMENT" })}>-</button>
    </div>
  );
}
```

The `initialView` prop is required — the server always provides the first snapshot. `useView()` returns the view directly, no null checks needed. The WebSocket connects and takes over with live updates.

## 4. Deploy

```bash
npx wrangler deploy
```

# Counter

Source: https://actorkit.dev/examples/counter/

The counter is the simplest actor — it demonstrates the contract-first API, flat messages, guards, views, and real-time sync between multiple users.

**Source**: [`examples/counter/`](https://github.com/actor-kit/actor-kit/tree/main/examples/counter)

## What it demonstrates

- `setup()` + `kit.actor()` + `createActorClass()` — contract-first API
- Flat messages with optional guards
- `kit.message()` with Zod validation
- `schema()` and `view.shared()` for typed view projections
- Real-time sync: two browsers sharing the same counter
- Admin vs user roles via `callerType`
- Contract-derived client: typed `actorClient(contract)` — no manual message unions

## The Contract

The contract defines state, messages, roles, and views in a single file:

```typescript
// counter.contract.ts
import { z } from "zod";
import { schema, view, uint32, string, nullable } from "@actor-kit/core";
import { setup } from "@actor-kit/worker";

type CounterState = { count: number; lastUpdatedBy: string | null };

const CounterView = schema({ count: uint32, lastUpdatedBy: nullable(string) });

// The kit: this actor declares no events, states or env, so it is empty.
const counter = setup({});

export const CounterContract = counter.actor("counter", {
  input: z.object({}),
  init: (): CounterState => ({ count: 0, lastUpdatedBy: null }),

  roles: {
    admin: (_state: CounterState, _caller: string, { callerType }: { callerType: "user" | "service" }) =>
      callerType === "service",
    user: () => true,
  },

  messages: {
    INCREMENT: counter.message(
      z.object({}),
      (state: CounterState, _payload, { caller }) => ({
        ...state,
        count: state.count + 1,
        lastUpdatedBy: caller,
      }),
    ),
    DECREMENT: counter.message(
      z.object({}),
      (state: CounterState, _payload, { caller }) => ({
        ...state,
        count: Math.max(0, state.count - 1),
        lastUpdatedBy: caller,
      }),
    ),
    RESET: counter.message(z.object({}), {
      guard: (_state: CounterState, _payload, ctx) => ctx.role === "admin",
      handler: () => ({ count: 0, lastUpdatedBy: null }),
    }),
  },

  views: {
    admin: view.shared(CounterView, (state: CounterState) => ({ count: state.count, lastUpdatedBy: state.lastUpdatedBy })),
    user: view.shared(CounterView, (state: CounterState) => ({ count: state.count, lastUpdatedBy: state.lastUpdatedBy })),
  },
});
export type CounterContract = typeof CounterContract;
```

## The Server

The server file imports the contract value and creates the Durable Object class:

```typescript
// counter.server.ts
import { createActorClass } from "@actor-kit/worker";
import { CounterContract } from "./counter.contract";

export const Counter = createActorClass(CounterContract);
```

Key points:
- **Messages are flat** — not nested by role. `RESET` uses a guard to restrict to admin
- **`counter.actor()`** returns a typed contract — `createActorClass()` converts it to a DO class
- **Both roles** can see `INCREMENT` and `DECREMENT` — guards are only needed for restricted actions
- **Views** are the same shape for both roles — in more complex actors, roles would see different projections
- **The contract is separate from the DO class** — server imports the value, client imports only the type

## The Worker

The Worker is the auth boundary. It derives caller identity from a session cookie (NOT from query params) and stamps it onto the request via `withCallerIdentity()` before forwarding to the DO:

```typescript
// src/worker.ts
import { withCallerIdentity } from "@actor-kit/worker";
import { Counter } from "./counter.server";

export { Counter };

interface Env {
  COUNTER: DurableObjectNamespace;
}

export default {
  async fetch(request: Request, env: Env): Promise<Response> {
    const url = new URL(request.url);

    if (url.pathname.startsWith("/api/counter/")) {
      const actorId = url.pathname.split("/")[3] ?? "default";

      // Authenticate via session cookie (PRODUCTION: validate a signed cookie, OAuth, etc.)
      const { callerId } = resolveCaller(request);

      const id = env.COUNTER.idFromName(actorId);
      const stub = env.COUNTER.get(id);

      // Spawn idempotently
      await stub.spawn({ actorId, caller: "system", callerType: "service", input: {} });

      // Stamp verified identity and forward to DO
      const stamped = withCallerIdentity(request, { callerId, callerType: "user" });
      return stub.fetch(stamped);
    }

    return new Response("Not found", { status: 404 });
  },
};

function resolveCaller(request: Request): { callerId: string } {
  const cookieHeader = request.headers.get("Cookie") ?? "";
  const match = cookieHeader.match(/(?:^|;\s*)caller_id=([^;]+)/);
  if (match?.[1]) return { callerId: decodeURIComponent(match[1]) };
  return { callerId: `user-${crypto.randomUUID().slice(0, 8)}` };
}
```

Note: `callerId` comes from the cookie — it is never accepted from the URL. Clients connect to `/api/counter/<id>` with no query params; the session cookie is sent automatically by the browser.

## The Client

### Vanilla TypeScript

Client code uses `import type` to import the contract — this keeps Zod, handlers, and Cloudflare dependencies out of the browser bundle. The client takes a `path` (not a full URL) and requires an `initialView` — the server always provides the first snapshot:

```typescript
import { actorClient } from "@actor-kit/client";
import type { CounterContract } from "./counter.contract";

// Type-only — no runtime contract value in the bundle
const CounterClient = actorClient<CounterContract>();

// Create a runtime connection — cookie is sent automatically by the browser
const client = CounterClient.create({
  path: `/api/counter/default`,
  initialView: { count: 0, lastUpdatedBy: "" }, // or an SSR snapshot
});
client.connect();

// view is typed: { count: number; lastUpdatedBy: string }
client.subscribe((view) => {
  document.getElementById("count")!.textContent = String(view.count);
});

client.send({ type: "INCREMENT" });
```

### React

The server fetches the initial snapshot during SSR. `useClient()` creates and manages the client's lifecycle — it opens the WebSocket on mount and closes it on unmount:

```tsx
import { actorContext } from "@actor-kit/react";
import type { CounterContract } from "./counter.contract";

// Type-only — no runtime contract value in the bundle
const CounterCtx = actorContext<typeof CounterContract>();

// Server loader: fetch initial snapshot from the Durable Object.
// Runs on the Worker — direct DO binding access.
export async function loader({ env, params }: { env: Env; params: { counterId: string } }) {
  const id = env.COUNTER.idFromName(params.counterId);
  const stub = env.COUNTER.get(id);
  await stub.spawn({
    actorId: params.counterId,
    caller: "system",
    callerType: "service",
    input: {},
  });
  const { snapshot } = await stub.getSnapshot("demo-user", "user");
  return { counterId: params.counterId, snapshot };
}

function App({ counterId, snapshot }: { counterId: string; snapshot: { count: number; lastUpdatedBy: string } }) {
  // useClient creates the client once (stable across re-renders) and manages
  // connect/disconnect. initialView seeds the view before the socket opens —
  // no undefined state. Cookies provide auth automatically.
  const client = CounterCtx.useClient({
    path: `/api/counter/${counterId}`,
    initialView: { role: "user", ...snapshot },
  });

  return (
    <CounterCtx.Provider client={client}>
      <Counter />
    </CounterCtx.Provider>
  );
}

function Counter() {
  const view = CounterCtx.useView();   // always defined — seeded from initialView
  const send = CounterCtx.useSend();

  return (
    <div>
      <span>{view.count}</span>
      <button onClick={() => send({ type: "INCREMENT" })}>+</button>
      <button onClick={() => send({ type: "DECREMENT" })}>-</button>
    </div>
  );
}
```

## Try it

```bash
cd examples/counter
pnpm install
pnpm dev
# Open http://localhost:8787
# Open a second tab — both see the same counter
```

# Todo List

Source: https://actorkit.dev/examples/todo-list/

The todo list demonstrates the role system in depth — different users see different views and have different permissions, all enforced through guards on flat messages.

**Source**: [`examples/todo-list/`](https://github.com/actor-kit/actor-kit/tree/main/examples/todo-list)

## What it demonstrates

- Three roles: `owner`, `member`, `viewer`
- Flat messages with guards for role-based authorization
- Per-role views: owner/member see todos, viewer sees counts
- Actor input: `ownerId` passed via `spawn()` to establish ownership
- `spawn()` for actors with required input (vs auto-spawn for no-input actors)
- State persistence across page reloads
- Client role detection: adapting UI based on `role` from the server

## Roles

```typescript
roles: {
  owner: (state: TodoState, caller: string) => caller === state.ownerId,
  member: (state: TodoState, caller: string) => state.memberIds.includes(caller),
  viewer: () => true,  // catch-all
},
```

Roles evaluate top-to-bottom. First match wins. If the caller is the owner, they get `owner` — even if they're also in `memberIds`.

## Flat Messages with Guards

The actor declares no events, states or env, so its kit is empty: `const todo = setup({})`, and the contract is `todo.actor("todo-list", { ... })`. Messages come from the kit:

```typescript
messages: {
  ADD_TODO: todo.message(
    z.object({ text: z.string().min(1).max(200) }),
    {
      guard: (_state: TodoState, _payload, ctx) => ctx.role === "owner" || ctx.role === "member",
      handler: (state: TodoState, { text }, ctx) => ({
        ...state,
        todos: [...state.todos, { id: ctx.id(), text, done: false }],
      }),
    },
  ),
  DELETE_TODO: todo.message(
    z.object({ id: z.string() }),
    {
      guard: (_state: TodoState, _payload, ctx) => ctx.role === "owner",
      handler: (state: TodoState, { id }) => ({
        ...state,
        todos: state.todos.filter((t) => t.id !== id),
      }),
    },
  ),
  TOGGLE: todo.message(
    z.object({ id: z.string() }),
    {
      guard: (_state: TodoState, _payload, ctx) => ctx.role === "owner" || ctx.role === "member",
      handler: (state: TodoState, { id }) => ({
        ...state,
        todos: state.todos.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)),
      }),
    },
  ),
  INVITE: todo.message(
    z.object({ userId: z.string() }),
    {
      guard: (_state: TodoState, _payload, ctx) => ctx.role === "owner",
      handler: (state: TodoState, { userId }) => ({
        ...state,
        memberIds: [...state.memberIds, userId],
      }),
    },
  ),
},
```

Messages are flat — all defined at the top level. Guards check `ctx.role` to enforce authorization. A viewer sending `DELETE_TODO` is refused with code `guard_failed` without the handler running.

## Per-Role Views

```typescript
views: {
  owner: view.shared(OwnerViewSchema, (state: TodoState) => ({
    todos: state.todos,
    memberCount: state.memberIds.length,
  })),
  member: view.shared(OwnerViewSchema, (state: TodoState) => ({
    todos: state.todos,
    memberCount: state.memberIds.length,
  })),
  viewer: view.shared(ViewerViewSchema, (state: TodoState) => ({
    todoCount: state.todos.length,
    doneCount: state.todos.filter(t => t.done).length,
  })),
},
```

The owner and member see the full todo list. The viewer sees only counts — the individual todo items are never sent.

## The Worker

Unlike the counter (which auto-initializes with no input), the todo list requires an `ownerId` at creation time. Use `spawn()` to pass input on first connection. Caller identity comes from a session cookie — never from URL query params:

```typescript
// Route WebSocket connections to the TodoList DO
if (url.pathname.startsWith("/api/todo-list/")) {
  const listId = url.pathname.split("/")[3] ?? "default";

  // Authenticate via session cookie (PRODUCTION: signed cookie or OAuth)
  const { callerId: userId } = resolveCaller(request);

  const id = env.TODO_LIST.idFromName(listId);
  const stub = env.TODO_LIST.get(id);

  // spawn() is idempotent — first call creates with input, subsequent calls are no-ops
  await stub.spawn({
    actorId: listId,
    caller: userId,
    callerType: "user",
    input: { ownerId: userId },
  });

  // Stamp verified identity and forward to DO
  const stamped = withCallerIdentity(request, { callerId: userId, callerType: "user" });
  return stub.fetch(stamped);
}

function resolveCaller(request: Request): { callerId: string } {
  const cookieHeader = request.headers.get("Cookie") ?? "";
  const match = cookieHeader.match(/(?:^|;\s*)caller_id=([^;]+)/);
  if (match?.[1]) return { callerId: decodeURIComponent(match[1]) };
  return { callerId: `user-${crypto.randomUUID().slice(0, 8)}` };
}
```

The `ownerId` from input flows into `init()`, which sets the initial state. Role predicates then use `state.ownerId` to resolve the `owner` role. After the first `spawn()`, the actor persists and restores from SQLite — no re-initialization needed.

## The Client

### Vanilla TypeScript

Client code uses `import type` to import the contract — this keeps Zod, handlers, and Cloudflare dependencies out of the browser bundle. Binary delta decoding is handled transparently — the `subscribe` callback always receives the full, merged view:

```typescript
import { actorClient } from "@actor-kit/client";
import type { TodoListContract } from "./todo.contract";

// Type-only — no runtime contract value in the bundle
const TodoClient = actorClient<TodoListContract>();

// Create a runtime connection — the browser sends the session cookie automatically
const client = TodoClient.create({
  path: `/api/todo-list/my-list`,
  initialView: { role: "viewer", todoCount: 0, doneCount: 0 }, // or an SSR snapshot
});
client.connect();

// view is a discriminated union — narrow by role before accessing role-specific fields
client.subscribe((view) => {
  if (view.role === "owner" || view.role === "member") {
    renderTodos(view.todos);
  } else {
    renderCounts(view.todoCount, view.doneCount);
  }
});

client.send({ type: "ADD_TODO", text: "Buy milk" });
```

### React

```tsx
import { actorContext } from "@actor-kit/react";
import type { TodoListContract } from "./todo.contract";

// Type-only — no runtime contract value in the bundle
const TodoCtx = actorContext<typeof TodoListContract>();

// Server loader: fetch the initial role-scoped snapshot from the DO
export async function loader({ env, params, callerId }: { env: Env; params: { listId: string }; callerId: string }) {
  const stub = env.TODO_LIST.get(env.TODO_LIST.idFromName(params.listId));
  await stub.spawn({
    actorId: params.listId,
    caller: callerId,
    callerType: "user",
    input: { ownerId: callerId },
  });
  const { snapshot, role } = await stub.getSnapshot(callerId, "user");
  return { listId: params.listId, snapshot, role };
}

function TodoApp({ listId, snapshot, role }: { listId: string; snapshot: unknown; role: string }) {
  // useClient creates the client once and manages connect/disconnect on mount.
  // Cookies supply caller identity — no callerId is needed on the client.
  const client = TodoCtx.useClient({
    path: `/api/todo-list/${listId}`,
    initialView: { role, ...(snapshot as object) } as never,
  });

  return (
    <TodoCtx.Provider client={client}>
      <TodoList />
    </TodoCtx.Provider>
  );
}

function TodoList() {
  const role = TodoCtx.useRole();
  const send = TodoCtx.useSend();

  // Use useSelector to safely extract what we need based on role
  const todos = TodoCtx.useSelector((view) => {
    if (view && 'todos' in view) return view.todos;
    return [];
  });

  const count = TodoCtx.useSelector((view) => {
    if (view && 'todoCount' in view) return view.todoCount;
    if (view && 'todos' in view) return view.todos.length;
    return 0;
  });

  if (role === "viewer") {
    return <div>{count} todos</div>;
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <ul>
        {todos.map(t => (
          <li key={t.id}>
            <span onClick={() => send({ type: "TOGGLE", id: t.id })}>
              {t.done ? "done" : "todo"} {t.text}
            </span>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
      <button onClick={() => send({ type: "ADD_TODO", text: "New item" })}>
        Add
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}
```

`useRole()` re-renders when the role changes — if the owner invites someone, their role shifts from `viewer` to `member` and the UI updates automatically. `useSelector()` safely narrows the view shape: viewers get `{ todoCount, doneCount }` while owners/members get `{ todos, memberCount }`, so accessing `view.todos` directly would crash for viewers.

## Try it

```bash
cd examples/todo-list
pnpm install
pnpm dev
# Open http://localhost:8787?user=alice (owner)
# Open http://localhost:8787?user=bob (viewer)
```

# Chat Room

Source: https://actorkit.dev/examples/chat-room/

The chat room demonstrates WebSocket lifecycle events and real-time broadcast to multiple connected users.

**Source**: [`examples/chat-room/`](https://github.com/actor-kit/actor-kit/tree/main/examples/chat-room)

## What it demonstrates

- `lifecycle.connect` / `lifecycle.disconnect` handlers
- Online user tracking
- Real-time message broadcast to all connected users
- Message history (last 50 messages)
- Contract-derived client: no manual message unions

## Lifecycle Events

```typescript
// The kit: this actor declares no events, states or env, so it is empty.
const chat = setup({});

export const ChatRoomContract = chat.actor("chat-room", {
  input: z.object({}),
  init: (): ChatState => ({ messages: [], onlineUsers: [] }),

  roles: {
    user: () => true,
  },

  messages: {
    SEND_MESSAGE: chat.message(
      z.object({ text: z.string().min(1).max(500) }),
      (state: ChatState, { text }, { caller, id, now }) => ({
        ...state,
        messages: [
          ...state.messages.slice(-49),
          { id: id(), author: caller, text, timestamp: now() },
        ],
      }),
    ),
  },

  views: {
    user: view.shared(ChatViewSchema, (state: ChatState) => ({
      messages: state.messages.map((m) => ({ id: m.id, author: m.author, text: m.text })),
      onlineCount: state.onlineUsers.length,
    })),
  },

  lifecycle: {
    connect: (state: ChatState, { caller }: LifecycleEvent) => {
      if (state.onlineUsers.includes(caller)) return state;
      return { ...state, onlineUsers: [...state.onlineUsers, caller] };
    },
    disconnect: (state: ChatState, { caller, callerConnections }: LifecycleEvent) => {
      if (callerConnections > 0) return state; // another tab is still open
      return { ...state, onlineUsers: state.onlineUsers.filter((u) => u !== caller) };
    },
  },
});
export type ChatRoomContract = typeof ChatRoomContract;

```

The server file imports the contract value and creates the DO class:

```typescript
// chat-room.server.ts
import { createActorClass } from "@actor-kit/worker";
import { ChatRoomContract } from "./chat.contract";

export const ChatRoom = createActorClass(ChatRoomContract);
```

When a WebSocket connects, the framework calls `lifecycle.connect` with `{ caller, callerType, callerConnections }`. When it disconnects, `lifecycle.disconnect` fires. Each socket (tab) is its own connection, so both fire once per tab; `callerConnections` is how many sockets that caller still has open after the event, so a user stays online until their last tab closes. Both are transitions — they persist state and broadcast views.

## Message Handling

The `.slice(-49)` keeps the last 50 messages — old messages are discarded to bound state size. Handlers are synchronous — no `async`/`await`.

## The Client

### Vanilla TypeScript

Client code uses `import type` to import the contract — this keeps Zod, handlers, and Cloudflare dependencies out of the browser bundle. Binary delta decoding is handled transparently — the `subscribe` callback always receives the full, merged view:

The Worker authenticates via session cookie and forwards to the DO with `withCallerIdentity()` — caller identity is never taken from URL params:

```typescript
if (url.pathname.startsWith("/api/chat-room/")) {
  const roomId = url.pathname.split("/")[3] ?? "general";
  const { callerId } = resolveCaller(request); // cookie-based
  const stub = env.CHAT_ROOM.get(env.CHAT_ROOM.idFromName(roomId));
  await stub.spawn({ actorId: roomId, caller: "system", callerType: "service", input: {} });
  const stamped = withCallerIdentity(request, { callerId, callerType: "user" });
  return stub.fetch(stamped);
}
```

```typescript
import { actorClient } from "@actor-kit/client";
import type { ChatRoomContract } from "./chat.contract";

// Type-only — no runtime contract value in the bundle
const ChatClient = actorClient<ChatRoomContract>();

// Create a runtime connection — cookies provide caller identity automatically
const client = ChatClient.create({
  path: `/api/chat-room/general`,
  initialView: { role: "user", messages: [], onlineCount: 0 }, // or an SSR snapshot
});
client.connect();

// view is typed from the contract's view schemas
client.subscribe((view) => {
  document.getElementById("online")!.textContent = `${view.onlineCount} online`;
  document.getElementById("messages")!.innerHTML = view.messages
    .map(m => `<div><b>${m.author}</b>: ${m.text}</div>`)
    .join("");
});

client.send({ type: "SEND_MESSAGE", text: "Hello!" });
```

### React

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { actorContext } from "@actor-kit/react";
import type { ChatRoomContract } from "./chat.contract";

// Type-only — no runtime contract value in the bundle
const ChatCtx = actorContext<typeof ChatRoomContract>();

// Server loader: fetch initial snapshot from the DO
export async function loader({ env, params, callerId }: { env: Env; params: { roomId: string }; callerId: string }) {
  const stub = env.CHAT_ROOM.get(env.CHAT_ROOM.idFromName(params.roomId));
  await stub.spawn({ actorId: params.roomId, caller: "system", callerType: "service", input: {} });
  const { snapshot } = await stub.getSnapshot(callerId, "user");
  return { roomId: params.roomId, snapshot };
}

function ChatApp({ roomId, snapshot }: { roomId: string; snapshot: { messages: { id: string; author: string; text: string }[]; onlineCount: number } }) {
  // useClient manages the WebSocket lifecycle. initialView seeds useView() so
  // there's no undefined loading state. Auth is via cookies — no callerId prop.
  const client = ChatCtx.useClient({
    path: `/api/chat-room/${roomId}`,
    initialView: { role: "user", ...snapshot },
  });

  return (
    <ChatCtx.Provider client={client}>
      <ChatRoom />
    </ChatCtx.Provider>
  );
}

function ChatRoom() {
  const view = ChatCtx.useView();   // typed from contract view schemas — always defined
  const send = ChatCtx.useSend();   // message types inferred from contract
  const [text, setText] = useState("");

  return (
    <div>
      <div>{view.onlineCount} online</div>
      <div>
        {view.messages.map(m => (
          <div key={m.id}><b>{m.author}</b>: {m.text}</div>
        ))}
      </div>
      <input value={text} onChange={e => setText(e.target.value)} />
      <button onClick={() => { send({ type: "SEND_MESSAGE", text }); setText(""); }}>
        Send
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}
```

The `lifecycle.connect` and `lifecycle.disconnect` handlers on the actor handle online tracking — the client doesn't need to do anything special. A user's first tab adds them to the count; closing their last tab removes them. Extra tabs of the same user do not change it.

## Try it

```bash
cd examples/chat-room
pnpm install
pnpm dev
# Open http://localhost:8787?user=alice
# Open http://localhost:8787?user=bob
# Both see messages in real-time + online count
```

# Auction

Source: https://actorkit.dev/examples/auction/

The auction demonstrates guards — conditions that reject messages before the handler runs.

**Source**: [`examples/auction/`](https://github.com/actor-kit/actor-kit/tree/main/examples/auction)

## What it demonstrates

- Guards on `auction.message()` to enforce business rules
- Guards checking both state and `ctx.role` for authorization
- Competitive real-time bidding between users
- Service-only actions (close auction) via `callerType` role
- Contract-derived client: no manual message unions

## Guards

```typescript
type Bid = { bidder: string; amount: number; timestamp: number };
type AuctionState = { item: string; bids: Bid[]; closed: boolean; winner: string | null; winningBid: number };

// The kit. The full example also declares domain events here (see Domain Events).
const auction = setup({});

export const AuctionContract = auction.actor("auction", {
  input: z.object({ item: z.string() }),
  init: (input: { item: string }): AuctionState => ({
    item: input.item, bids: [], closed: false, winner: null, winningBid: 0,
  }),

  roles: {
    auctioneer: (_state: AuctionState, _caller: string, { callerType }: { callerType: "user" | "service" }) =>
      callerType === "service",
    bidder: () => true,
  },

  messages: {
    BID: auction.message(z.object({ amount: z.number().int().positive() }), {
      guard: (state: AuctionState) => !state.closed,
      handler: (state: AuctionState, { amount }, { caller, now }) => {
        const highest = state.bids.length > 0
          ? Math.max(...state.bids.map(b => b.amount))
          : 0;
        if (amount <= highest) return state;  // Reject lower bids silently
        return {
          ...state,
          bids: [...state.bids, { bidder: caller, amount, timestamp: now() }],
        };
      },
    }),
    CLOSE: auction.message(z.object({}), {
      guard: (state: AuctionState, _payload, ctx) =>
        ctx.role === "auctioneer" && !state.closed && state.bids.length > 0,
      handler: (state: AuctionState) => {
        const winner = state.bids.reduce((best, b) =>
          b.amount > best.amount ? b : best, state.bids[0]!
        );
        return { ...state, closed: true, winner: winner.bidder, winningBid: winner.amount };
      },
    }),
  },

  views: {
    // Auctioneer sees all bids with bidder names + revenue
    auctioneer: view.shared(AuctioneerView, (state: AuctionState) => ({
      item: state.item,
      bids: state.bids,
      bidCount: state.bids.length,
      highestBid: Math.max(0, ...state.bids.map(b => b.amount)),
      revenue: state.closed ? state.winningBid : 0,
      closed: state.closed,
      winner: state.winner ?? "",
    })),
    // Bidders see bid count and highest bid — not who bid
    bidder: view.shared(BidderView, (state: AuctionState) => ({
      item: state.item,
      bidCount: state.bids.length,
      highestBid: Math.max(0, ...state.bids.map(b => b.amount)),
      closed: state.closed,
      winner: state.winner ?? "",
    })),
  },
});
export type AuctionContract = typeof AuctionContract;

```

The server file imports the contract value and creates the DO class:

```typescript
// auction.server.ts
import { createActorClass } from "@actor-kit/worker";
import { AuctionContract } from "./auction.contract";

export const Auction = createActorClass(AuctionContract);
```

Key points:
- **BID guard** checks state only: `!state.closed` — any role can bid when open
- **CLOSE guard** checks both state and role: `ctx.role === "auctioneer" && !state.closed && state.bids.length > 0`
- Guards run before the handler. If the guard returns `false`, the message is refused with code `guard_failed` — the handler never executes
- Inside the BID handler, the amount check is business logic (not a guard) — it returns unchanged state instead of throwing

## The Client

### Vanilla TypeScript

Client code uses `import type` to import the contract — this keeps Zod, handlers, and Cloudflare dependencies out of the browser bundle. Binary delta decoding is handled transparently — the `subscribe` callback always receives the full, merged view:

The Worker authenticates via session cookie and stamps identity with `withCallerIdentity()` — the auctioneer role is granted based on `callerType: "service"`, not on URL params.

```typescript
import { actorClient } from "@actor-kit/client";
import type { AuctionContract } from "./auction.contract";

// Type-only — no runtime contract value in the bundle
const AuctionClient = actorClient<AuctionContract>();

// Create a runtime connection — the browser sends the session cookie automatically
const client = AuctionClient.create({
  path: `/api/auction/my-auction`,
  initialView: {
    role: "bidder",
    item: "",
    bidCount: 0,
    highestBid: 0,
    closed: false,
    winner: "",
  }, // or an SSR snapshot
});
client.connect();

// view is typed from the contract's view schemas
client.subscribe((view) => {
  document.getElementById("highest")!.textContent = String(view.highestBid);
  document.getElementById("count")!.textContent = `${view.bidCount} bids`;

  if (view.closed) {
    document.getElementById("bid-form")!.hidden = true;
    document.getElementById("winner")!.textContent = `Winner: ${view.winner}`;
  }
});

client.send({ type: "BID", amount: 100 });
```

### React

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { actorContext } from "@actor-kit/react";
import type { LinkedView } from "@actor-kit/core";
import type { AuctionContract } from "./auction.contract";

type AuctionView = LinkedView<typeof AuctionContract>;

// Type-only — no runtime contract value in the bundle
const AuctionCtx = actorContext<typeof AuctionContract>();

// Server loader: fetch the role-scoped initial snapshot from the DO
export async function loader({ env, params, callerId }: { env: Env; params: { auctionId: string }; callerId: string }) {
  const stub = env.AUCTION.get(env.AUCTION.idFromName(params.auctionId));
  await stub.spawn({
    actorId: params.auctionId,
    caller: "system",
    callerType: "service",
    input: { item: "Vintage poster" },
  });
  const { snapshot, role } = await stub.getSnapshot(callerId, "user");
  return { auctionId: params.auctionId, snapshot, role };
}

function AuctionApp({ auctionId, snapshot, role }: { auctionId: string; snapshot: object; role: string }) {
  // useClient manages connect/disconnect on mount. Cookies supply auth,
  // so no callerId is needed on the client.
  const client = AuctionCtx.useClient({
    path: `/api/auction/${auctionId}`,
    initialView: { role, ...snapshot } as never,
  });

  return (
    <AuctionCtx.Provider client={client}>
      <Auction />
    </AuctionCtx.Provider>
  );
}

function Auction() {
  const view = AuctionCtx.useView();
  // view type is a discriminated union:
  // | { role: "auctioneer"; item; bids; bidCount; highestBid; revenue; closed; winner }
  // | { role: "bidder";     item; bidCount; highestBid; closed; winner }

  // view is always defined — initialView seeds it before the socket opens.

  // Common fields — accessible without narrowing (exist on ALL role variants)
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>{view.item}</h1>
      <div>Highest bid: ${view.highestBid} ({view.bidCount} bids)</div>

      {/* Role-specific UI — narrow with view.role */}
      {view.role === "auctioneer" && <AuctioneerPanel view={view} />}
      {view.role === "bidder" && <BidderPanel view={view} />}
    </div>
  );
}

// TypeScript narrows the view type in each component:

function AuctioneerPanel({ view }: { view: Extract<AuctionView, { role: "auctioneer" }> }) {
  const send = AuctionCtx.useSend();
  // view.bids and view.revenue are available — TS knows this is the auctioneer variant
  return (
    <div>
      <div>Revenue: ${view.revenue}</div>
      <div>{view.bids.length} bids from {new Set(view.bids.map(b => b.bidder)).size} bidders</div>
      {!view.closed && (
        <button onClick={() => send({ type: "CLOSE" })}>Close Auction</button>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

function BidderPanel({ view }: { view: Extract<AuctionView, { role: "bidder" }> }) {
  const send = AuctionCtx.useSend();
  const [amount, setAmount] = useState(0);
  // view.bids is NOT available here — TS correctly excludes it from the bidder variant
  return view.closed ? (
    <div>Winner: {view.winner}</div>
  ) : (
    <div>
      <input type="number" value={amount} onChange={e => setAmount(+e.target.value)} />
      <button onClick={() => send({ type: "BID", amount })}>Place Bid</button>
    </div>
  );
}
```

**Role narrowing works because every view push includes a `role` discriminant.** Common fields (`item`, `bidCount`, `highestBid`, `closed`, `winner`) are accessible on the union without narrowing. Role-specific fields (`bids`, `revenue`) require narrowing via `view.role`.

You can also use `useSelector` with a role for fine-grained subscriptions:

```tsx
// Only re-renders when revenue changes — and only if you're the auctioneer
const revenue = AuctionCtx.useSelector("auctioneer", (v) => v.revenue);

// Common fields work without a role
const bidCount = AuctionCtx.useSelector((v) => v?.bidCount ?? 0);
```

When the auction closes (via the `auctioneer` service role), all connected clients receive the updated view with `closed: true` and the winner — the UI adapts automatically.

## Try it

```bash
cd examples/auction
pnpm install
pnpm dev
# Open http://localhost:8787?user=alice
# Open http://localhost:8787?user=bob
# Both bid — highest bid wins
```

## Related

- [Messages & Guards](https://actorkit.dev/concepts/messages-and-guards/) — how guards validate messages before the handler runs
- [Testing](https://actorkit.dev/concepts/testing/) — test actors with `testActor()` to verify guard and handler behavior

# Actors & State

Source: https://actorkit.dev/concepts/actors-and-state/

## The Actor Model

An actor is a unit of computation with:
- **A mailbox** — messages arrive and are processed one at a time
- **Private state** — only the actor can read/write its state
- **Behavior** — a function from (state, message) → new state

In Actor Kit, each actor is a Cloudflare Durable Object. DOs are single-threaded and globally addressable — they're natural actors.

## Defining an Actor

```typescript
import { z } from "zod";
import { createActorClass, setup } from "@actor-kit/worker";

// The kit: what the actor declares up front — events, states, env (all optional).
const myActor = setup({});

export const MyActorContract = myActor.actor("my-actor", {
  input: z.object({ name: z.string() }),
  init: (input: { name: string }) => ({
    name: input.name,
    count: 0,
  }),
  roles: { /* ... */ },
  messages: { /* myActor.message(...) */ },
  views: { /* ... */ },
});
export type MyActorContract = typeof MyActorContract;

export const MyActor = createActorClass(MyActorContract);
```

`setup()` returns the kit: the actor's declarations (`events`, `states`, `env`) and the helpers typed by them (`myActor.message()`, `myActor.timer()`, `myActor.in(state)`). `myActor.actor()` returns a typed contract — not a DO class. The contract preserves all type information (state, messages, views, roles) for downstream consumers (`actorClient`, `actorContext`, `testActor`). `createActorClass()` converts the contract into a Durable Object class.

### `input`

A Zod schema that validates the data provided when the actor is first created (`spawn`). Invalid input is rejected — the actor is never created.

### `init(input)`

Returns the initial state. The return type is inferred — no manual type annotations needed.

### `versions`

A typed chain of state versions (ADR-015). Each version names the schema of the persisted state at that version and
how to get there from the previous one:

```typescript
import { version } from "@actor-kit/worker";

const V1 = z.object({ players: z.array(z.string()) });
const V2 = z.object({ players: z.array(z.object({ id: z.string() })) });
const V3 = z.object({ players: z.array(z.object({ id: z.string(), avatar: z.string().nullable() })) });

versions: [
  version(1, V1),
  version(2, V2, {
    state: (s: z.infer<typeof V1>) => ({ players: s.players.map((id) => ({ id })) }),
    events: { JOIN: (payload) => ({ ...payload, avatar: null }) },
  }),
  version(3, V3, { rebuild: "replay" }),
],
```

- **`state`** steps the previous version's state to this one. Its argument is typed by the previous version: a step
  that takes the wrong shape, or a last version that does not describe what `init` returns, is a type error.
- **`events`** upcasts message payloads journaled before this version, by message name, when the journal is replayed.
- **`rebuild: "replay"`** rebuilds the state by replaying the whole journal under the new handlers (older payloads
  upcast) instead of stepping it. It needs the journal.

When an actor wakes with state stored by an older version, it is parsed with that version's schema, stepped (or
rebuilt) to the current version, and journaled as a `migrate` event with a checkpoint. From then on the journal
replays from that bump; `replayJournal()` refuses events written by a version that is not in the chain. Without
`versions`, an actor is at version 1. The old `version` / `migrate` options are refused.

## Time and randomness

Handlers are replayed from the journal, so they read time and randomness only through `ctx.now()`,
`ctx.random()` and `ctx.id()`: the journal records what they returned, and replay hands the same values
back. Reading the globals directly (`Date.now()`, `new Date()`, `performance.now()`, `Math.random()`,
`crypto.randomUUID()`, `crypto.getRandomValues()`) is caught three ways:

- **In tests** (`testActor`, `simulate`, `replayJournal`) every such call throws a `NondeterminismError`.
- **In production** the actor's `determinism` option decides. `"warn"` (the default) lets the call
  return the real value, logs one `actor_kit.handler.nondeterministic` line naming what was called and
  what to use instead, and flags the journal entry `nondeterministic` (Studio's timeline shows a badge).
  `"throw"` fails the transition as in tests; `"off"` patches nothing.

```typescript
export const Game = game.actor("game", { determinism: "throw", ... });
```

- **In your editor and CI** with the Biome plugin that ships in `@actor-kit/worker`. It flags those calls
  inside `message()` / `timer()` handlers and the `onDone`, `onError`, `onUpdate`, `onUnlink`, `connect`,
  `disconnect`, `enter` and `init` callbacks (a service's `fn` is not a handler and may use them):

```json
{ "plugins": ["./node_modules/@actor-kit/worker/biome/no-nondeterminism.grit"] }
```

Silence a line on purpose with `// biome-ignore lint/plugin: <why>`.

## Persistence

State is automatically persisted to DO SQLite after every transition. When the DO restarts (after hibernation or a deploy), state is restored.

### Custom Serialization

If your state contains non-JSON-safe values (Maps, Sets, Dates), provide custom serializers:

```typescript
serialize: (state) => ({
  ...state,
  createdAt: state.createdAt.toISOString(),
}),
restore: (serialized) => ({
  ...serialized,
  createdAt: new Date(serialized.createdAt),
}),
```

## Spawning Actors

Whether you need to explicitly spawn an actor depends on its `input` schema.

### Auto-spawn (no required input)

Actors with no required input auto-initialize on the first `fetch()` — no `spawn()` call needed:

```typescript
input: z.object({}),
init: () => ({ count: 0 }),
```

When a client connects via WebSocket or sends an HTTP request, the actor initializes automatically if it doesn't already exist.

### Explicit spawn (required input)

Actors with required input must be spawned with `spawn({ input })` before any client can connect. This is for actors whose initial state depends on data provided at creation time:

```typescript
input: z.object({ ownerId: z.string(), title: z.string() }),
init: (input) => ({ ownerId: input.ownerId, title: input.title, items: [] }),
```

```typescript
const id = env.MY_ACTOR.idFromName("actor-123");
const stub = env.MY_ACTOR.get(id);
await stub.spawn({
  actorId: "actor-123",
  caller: "user-1",
  callerType: "user",
  input: { ownerId: "user-1", title: "My List" },
});
```

### Idempotency

`spawn()` is idempotent — calling it on an already-initialized actor is a no-op. This means it's safe to call `spawn()` every time before connecting, without checking whether the actor already exists.

## Lifecycle Events

The `lifecycle` block handles WebSocket connection events:

```typescript
lifecycle: {
  connect: (state, { caller, callerConnections }) => {
    if (callerConnections > 1) return state; // already online in another tab
    return { ...state, onlineUsers: [...state.onlineUsers, caller] };
  },
  disconnect: (state, { caller, callerConnections }) => {
    if (callerConnections > 0) return state; // another tab is still open
    return { ...state, onlineUsers: state.onlineUsers.filter(u => u !== caller) };
  },
},
```

`connect` and `disconnect` fire when WebSocket connections open and close — once per socket, so a user with two tabs connects twice. The event is `{ caller, callerType, callerConnections }`, where `callerConnections` is how many sockets that caller has open after the event (the first connect sees 1, the last disconnect sees 0). Both are full transitions — they persist state and broadcast views. Lifecycle handlers are synchronous — they return new state, not a Promise.

## Observability

The optional `observe.onTransition` hook fires after every successful state transition:

```typescript
observe: {
  onTransition(prevState, nextState, event, ctx) {
    console.log(`[${ctx.role}] ${event.type}: state changed`);
  },
},
```

This is useful for logging, metrics, or debugging. It also fires during `testActor()` tests.

## Related

- [Side Effects](https://actorkit.dev/concepts/side-effects/) — `execute()` and services for external communication

# Authentication

Source: https://actorkit.dev/concepts/authentication/

Actor Kit doesn't handle authentication. Your Worker authenticates the caller using whatever system you already have (sessions, OAuth, API keys, etc.) and stamps verified identity via `withCallerIdentity()` before forwarding the request to the Durable Object. The DO trusts the Worker.

The client SDK is auth-agnostic — it just opens a WebSocket. Three transport mechanisms cover the common deployment scenarios:

| Method | Same-origin web | Cross-origin web | Native mobile |
|--------|----------------|------------------|---------------|
| **Cookies** (existing session) | ✓ Recommended | ⚠ Requires CORS | ⚠ Manual cookie jar |
| **`getToken`** (Sec-WebSocket-Protocol) | ✓ Works | ✓ Recommended | ✓ Works |
| **`getHeaders`** (HTTP headers) | ✗ Browser API doesn't allow | ✗ Browser API doesn't allow | ✓ Recommended |

## Recommended: cookies (same-origin web)

When your web app is served from the same origin as your Worker AND the user already has a session cookie set (from a prior login flow, OAuth callback, etc.), the browser includes the cookie on the WebSocket upgrade request. The Worker reads the session cookie, validates it, and stamps caller identity. **No client SDK code is needed for auth — the browser is already sending it.**

This isn't magic — your auth flow must set the cookie before the user reaches the page that opens the WebSocket. A typical flow:

1. User logs in via your auth route → Worker sets a session cookie via `Set-Cookie`
2. User navigates to a page that opens an Actor Kit WebSocket
3. The browser includes the cookie in the upgrade request
4. The Worker reads it, validates the session, stamps identity, forwards to the DO

### Client

```typescript
const client = CounterClient.create({
  url: `wss://${location.host}/api/counter/my-counter`,
  initialView: snapshot,
});
```

That's the entire client. No auth code, no token plumbing, no headers — because the cookie is already there.

If the cookie isn't set (user not logged in, expired session), the Worker rejects the upgrade with 401 and the SDK's `onError` fires. Use `getToken` or `getHeaders` if your auth token isn't in cookies when the WebSocket connects (see below).

### Worker

```typescript
import { withCallerIdentity } from "@actor-kit/worker";

export default {
  async fetch(request: Request, env: Env) {
    // Read session from cookie — your auth library handles this
    const session = await getSession(request);
    if (!session) return new Response("Unauthorized", { status: 401 });

    const stub = env.COUNTER.get(env.COUNTER.idFromName("my-counter"));
    const stamped = withCallerIdentity(request, {
      callerId: session.userId,
      callerType: "user",
    });
    return stub.fetch(stamped);
  },
};
```

The browser sends the cookie automatically. The Worker validates the session. The DO trusts the Worker. The client SDK has no auth code.

This is the simplest pattern and works for the vast majority of web apps.

## Cross-origin web: `getToken` (Sec-WebSocket-Protocol)

When your web app is served from a different origin than your Worker, cookies don't automatically flow without CORS configuration. And the WebSocket browser API doesn't allow custom headers like `Authorization: Bearer ...`. The standard workaround is `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, a header that's part of the WebSocket upgrade handshake.

### Client

Pass a `getToken()` function. The SDK calls it before each connection (so refreshed tokens work on reconnect):

```typescript
const client = CounterClient.create({
  url: `wss://api.example.com/counter/my-counter`,
  initialView: snapshot,
  getToken: async () => session.accessToken,
});
```

The token can be anything — JWT, opaque session ID, signed string. The SDK doesn't care; it just transports the value.

### Worker

```typescript
import { withCallerIdentity, getTokenFromRequest } from "@actor-kit/worker";

export default {
  async fetch(request: Request, env: Env) {
    const token = getTokenFromRequest(request);
    if (!token) return new Response("Unauthorized", { status: 401 });

    // Your token validation
    const session = await validateToken(token);
    if (!session) return new Response("Unauthorized", { status: 401 });

    const stub = env.COUNTER.get(env.COUNTER.idFromName("my-counter"));
    const stamped = withCallerIdentity(request, {
      callerId: session.userId,
      callerType: "user",
    });
    return stub.fetch(stamped);
  },
};
```

`getTokenFromRequest()` extracts the token from the WebSocket upgrade headers. The library doesn't validate the token — that's your responsibility.

#### Why this works (under the hood)

The WebSocket protocol requires the server to acknowledge any subprotocol the client requests. When you use `getToken`, the SDK sends:

```
Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: actor-kit.v1, auth.<token>
```

The Actor Kit DO upgrade handler picks `actor-kit.v1` and echoes it back in the upgrade response — your Worker code doesn't need to do anything. Just call `withCallerIdentity()` and forward to the DO. The framework handles the protocol negotiation internally.

## Native mobile: `getHeaders`

Native WebSocket implementations (React Native's WebSocket, iOS `URLSessionWebSocketTask`, etc.) support setting arbitrary HTTP headers on the upgrade request. The SDK accepts a `getHeaders()` option for native clients.

```typescript
// React Native
const client = CounterClient.create({
  url: `wss://api.example.com/counter/my-counter`,
  initialView: snapshot,
  getHeaders: async () => ({
    Authorization: `Bearer ${await myAuth.getAccessToken()}`,
  }),
});
```

The SDK passes these headers to the underlying WebSocket implementation. Browser WebSocket clients ignore this option (the browser API doesn't allow custom WebSocket headers). The SDK throws a clear error if you try to use `getHeaders` in a browser context.

### Worker

Read whatever header you set:

```typescript
import { withCallerIdentity } from "@actor-kit/worker";

export default {
  async fetch(request: Request, env: Env) {
    const auth = request.headers.get("Authorization");
    const token = auth?.replace(/^Bearer /, "");
    if (!token) return new Response("Unauthorized", { status: 401 });

    const session = await validateToken(token);
    if (!session) return new Response("Unauthorized", { status: 401 });

    const stub = env.COUNTER.get(env.COUNTER.idFromName("my-counter"));
    const stamped = withCallerIdentity(request, {
      callerId: session.userId,
      callerType: "user",
    });
    return stub.fetch(stamped);
  },
};
```

## Server side: `withCallerIdentity()`

Regardless of which auth method you use, the Worker always wraps the request with verified identity before forwarding to the DO:

```typescript
const stamped = withCallerIdentity(request, {
  callerId: session.userId,
  callerType: "user",
});
return stub.fetch(stamped);
```

This:

- **Scrubs** any inbound `X-Actor-Kit-Caller-*` headers — prevents clients from spoofing identity by setting headers themselves
- **Stamps** the verified identity as headers the DO trusts
- **Forwards** the request to the DO

The DO is intentionally dumb — it trusts whatever identity the Worker stamps. All auth logic lives in your Worker, where you have full control over session validation, OAuth flows, refresh tokens, API keys, rate limiting, and so on.

## Choosing a method

```
┌─ Same origin? ──── Yes ──→ Use cookies (no client code)
│
└─ Different origin?
   │
   ├─ Browser? ──── Yes ──→ Use getToken (Sec-WebSocket-Protocol)
   │
   └─ Native (React Native, iOS)? ──→ Use getHeaders (Authorization header)
```

You can also mix methods. The Worker can accept both cookies and tokens, falling back from one to the other:

```typescript
async fetch(request, env) {
  const session =
    (await getSessionFromCookie(request)) ??
    (await getSessionFromToken(getTokenFromRequest(request)));

  if (!session) return new Response("Unauthorized", { status: 401 });
  // ... withCallerIdentity, forward to DO
}
```

## What the SDK doesn't do

- **No JWT minting** — bring your own token format
- **No session storage** — your auth library handles that
- **No CSRF protection** — your Worker handles it
- **No refresh logic** — `getToken()` is called on every connect, so you implement refresh inside your auth code

The SDK is a transport. Your Worker is the gatekeeper.

## Related

- [Roles & Authorization](https://actorkit.dev/concepts/roles-and-authorization/) — once a caller is authenticated, roles determine what they can do inside an actor
- [withCallerIdentity API](https://actorkit.dev/api/worker/) — full API reference

# Roles & Authorization

Source: https://actorkit.dev/concepts/roles-and-authorization/

## Roles Are Derived from State

Roles are not stored in tokens or databases. They're computed from the current state every time a message arrives.

```typescript
roles: {
  owner: (state, caller) => caller === state.ownerId,
  member: (state, caller) => state.memberIds.includes(caller),
  viewer: () => true,
},
```

### First Match Wins

Roles evaluate top-to-bottom. The first predicate that returns `true` determines the caller's role.

If a caller is both the owner AND a member, they get `owner` — because it's listed first.

### No Match = Rejection

If no role predicate returns `true`, the connection is rejected with a 403. Every actor should have a catch-all role (like `viewer: () => true`) or explicitly reject unknown callers.

### Re-Evaluated on Every Message

Roles are not cached. When the state changes, a caller's role can change too. This enables dynamic authorization:

```typescript
// A todo list where anyone who adds a todo becomes a member
ADD_TODO: todo.message(z.object({ text: z.string() }), {
  guard: (_state: TodoState, _payload, ctx) => ctx.role === "owner" || ctx.role === "member",
  handler: (state: TodoState, { text }, { caller }) => ({
    ...state,
    todos: [...state.todos, { text, done: false }],
    memberIds: [...new Set([...state.memberIds, caller])],
  }),
}),
```

After adding a todo, the caller's role changes from `viewer` to `member` on the next message.

## callerType

The caller identity includes a `callerType` field — either `"user"` or `"service"`. This is stable identity metadata set by the Worker via `withCallerIdentity()`, not dynamic authorization.

```typescript
roles: {
  service: (_state: State, _caller: string, { callerType }: { callerType: "user" | "service" }) =>
    callerType === "service",
  user: () => true,
},
```

Use `callerType` to distinguish backend services from browser users. Use roles for everything else.

## Flat Messages with Guards

Messages are flat — not nested by role. Authorization is enforced through guards (`todo` is the actor's kit, `setup({})`):

```typescript
messages: {
  ADD_TODO: todo.message(z.object({ text: z.string() }), {
    guard: (_state: TodoState, _payload, ctx) => ctx.role === "owner" || ctx.role === "member",
    handler: (state: TodoState, { text }) => ({ ...state, todos: [...state.todos, { text, done: false }] }),
  }),
  DELETE_TODO: todo.message(z.object({ id: z.string() }), {
    guard: (_state: TodoState, _payload, ctx) => ctx.role === "owner",
    handler: (state: TodoState, { id }) => ({ ...state, todos: state.todos.filter(t => t.id !== id) }),
  }),
  // No guard = open to all roles
  VIEW_COUNT: todo.message(z.object({}), (state: TodoState) => state),
},
```

If a `viewer` sends `DELETE_TODO`, the guard returns `false` and the message is refused with code `guard_failed` — the handler never runs. Messages without guards are open to all roles.

## Per-Role Views

Each role sees a different projection of the state:

```typescript
views: {
  owner: view.shared(OwnerView, (state: TodoState) => ({ todos: state.todos, settings: state.settings })),
  viewer: view.shared(ViewerView, (state: TodoState) => ({ todoCount: state.todos.length })),
},
```

The viewer never receives the actual todo items — only the count.

## Related

- [Messages & Guards](https://actorkit.dev/concepts/messages-and-guards/) — how messages are validated and guarded
- [FAQ](https://actorkit.dev/faq/) — common questions about role resolution and authorization

# Messages & Guards

Source: https://actorkit.dev/concepts/messages-and-guards/

## Messages

Every message handler is wrapped in the kit's `message()` — pairing a Zod schema with a handler function. The kit comes from `setup()`, which holds what the actor declares up front (events, states, env); an actor with none of them uses `setup({})`.

```typescript
import { setup } from "@actor-kit/worker";
import { z } from "zod";

const todo = setup({});

const addTodo = todo.message(
  z.object({ text: z.string().min(1).max(200) }),
  (state: TodoState, { text }, ctx) => ({
    ...state,
    todos: [...state.todos, { id: ctx.id(), text, done: false }],
  }),
);
```

Annotate the state type once, on the handler's first parameter. The payload is inferred from the schema, and `ctx` (including `env` and a typed `emit`) is typed by the kit.

### Flat Messages

Messages are defined at the top level — not nested by role. Authorization goes in guards:

```typescript
messages: {
  ADD_TODO: addTodo,                          // No guard = open to all roles
  DELETE_TODO: todo.message(z.object({ id: z.string() }), {
    guard: (_state: TodoState, _payload, ctx) => ctx.role === "owner",
    handler: (state: TodoState, { id }) => ({
      ...state,
      todos: state.todos.filter(t => t.id !== id),
    }),
  }),
},
```

### Roles on messages

**A message without `roles` is accepted from every role** (flat top-level messages and state messages
alike: a state message is found by the actor's current state, not by the caller's role). To limit who
may send one, name the roles; any other role is refused with `wrong_role` before the payload is parsed or
the guard runs:

```typescript
DRAW: playing.message(z.object({}), {
  roles: ["player"],                 // a guest or the TV cannot draw
  guard: (s: Shared, _p, ctx) => isTheirTurn(s, ctx.caller),
  handler: (s: Shared, _p, ctx) => draw(s, ctx.caller),
}),
```

Every name in `roles` must be one of the actor's roles: a typo is a definition error
(`invalid_actor_definition`) when the actor is created, in the Worker, `simulate()` and `testActor()`.

### Validation at the Boundary

The Zod schema runs `safeParse` on every incoming payload **before** the handler executes. If validation fails:
- The handler never runs
- The message is refused with code `invalid_payload` (the client receives an `__error` frame; `details` holds the Zod issues)
- State is unchanged

### Handler Signature

```typescript
(state: TState, payload: TPayload, ctx: MessageContext) => TState
```

- **`state`** — current actor state (immutable — return a new object)
- **`payload`** — Zod-validated payload
- **`ctx`** — context with `caller`, `callerType`, `role`, `env`, `execute`, `emit`, `schedule`, `now()`/`id()`/`random()` (and `phase`, `local`, `stay`, `goto` in a state's message)

Handlers are synchronous — they return new state, not a Promise. External I/O goes through `execute()` → services. See [Side Effects](https://actorkit.dev/concepts/side-effects/).

## Guards

Guards are optional conditions on messages. If the guard returns `false`, the message is rejected before the handler runs.

```typescript
const placeBid = auction.message(
  z.object({ amount: z.number().positive() }),
  {
    guard: (state: AuctionState) => !state.closed,
    handler: (state: AuctionState, { amount }, { caller }) => ({
      ...state,
      bids: [...state.bids, { bidder: caller, amount }],
    }),
  },
);
```

Guards receive `(state, payload, ctx)` where `ctx` includes `role`, `caller`, and `callerType`. This enables three kinds of guards:

- **State guards**: `(state) => !state.closed` — is this action allowed right now?
- **Role guards**: `(_state, _payload, ctx) => ctx.role === "owner"` — is this caller authorized?
- **Payload guards**: `(state, payload) => state.count + payload.amount <= 100` — is this specific data valid given current state?

### Evaluation Order

```
1. Resolve role → reject if no match (403 on connect, no_role on send)
2. Find the message for the role (and the current state) → unknown_message or wrong_state if none
   Check the message's roles, if it names any → wrong_role
3. Validate payload with Zod → invalid_payload if invalid
4. Evaluate guard(state, payload, ctx) → guard_failed if false
5. Run handler
```

## Refusals

A rejected message is a refusal: `{ ok: false, code, message, expected?, details?, docs }`. `message` is a full sentence naming the fix, `expected` lists what would have been accepted, `details` carries the specifics, and `docs` links to `https://actorkit.dev/errors/<code>/`. RPC `send()` returns it; over WebSocket the client receives an `__error` frame, `{ type: "__error", messageType, code, message, expected?, details?, docs }`, and `onError` gets those fields.

| Step | Failure | `code` |
|------|---------|--------|
| Role resolution | No role matches | Connection rejected (403); `no_role` on `send()` |
| Message lookup | The role has no message of that name | `unknown_message` (`expected`: the names it can send) |
| Message lookup | Only other states accept it | `wrong_state` (`expected`: those states, `details.phase`: the current one) |
| Message roles | The message names roles, and the caller's is not one | `wrong_role` (`expected`: those roles, `details.role`: the caller's) |
| Zod validation | Payload doesn't match schema | `invalid_payload` (`details`: the Zod issues) |
| Guard | Guard returns false | `guard_failed` |
| Handler | Handler throws | Error logged server-side; state unchanged |

The actor's state is never modified when a message is rejected.

## Related

- [Side Effects](https://actorkit.dev/concepts/side-effects/) — `execute()` and services for triggering effects from message handlers
- [Testing](https://actorkit.dev/concepts/testing/) — verify message validation, guards, and handler behavior with `testActor()`

# Views

Source: https://actorkit.dev/concepts/views/

## What is a View?

A view is a projection of the actor's state for a specific role. Different roles can see different data from the same actor.

```typescript
import { view, schema, uint32, string, array } from "@actor-kit/core";

const OwnerView = schema({ todos: array(TodoItem), memberCount: uint32 });
const ViewerView = schema({ todoCount: uint32, doneCount: uint32 });

views: {
  owner: view.shared(OwnerView, (state) => ({
    todos: state.todos,
    memberCount: state.memberIds.length,
  })),
  viewer: view.shared(ViewerView, (state) => ({
    todoCount: state.todos.length,
    doneCount: state.todos.filter(t => t.done).length,
  })),
},
```

## Schema

`schema()` defines the shape of the view for both TypeScript type inference and binary encoding:

```typescript
const PlayerView = schema({
  x: float32,
  y: float32,
  health: uint32,
  name: string,
  alive: boolean,
});

type PlayerViewType = Infer<typeof PlayerView>;
// { x: number; y: number; health: number; name: string; alive: boolean }
```

### Primitives

| Type | Bytes | TypeScript |
|------|-------|------------|
| `uint8` | 1 | `number` |
| `uint16` | 2 | `number` |
| `uint32` | 4 | `number` |
| `float32` | 4 | `number` |
| `float64` | 8 | `number` |
| `string` | 2 + UTF-8 | `string` |
| `boolean` | 1 | `boolean` |

### Combinators

- `array(T)` — array of any schema type
- `nullable(T)` — field that can be `null` (adds a compact null bitmask to the wire format)
- Nested `schema({...})` — objects within objects

## Binary Sync

Views defined with `view.shared(schema, fn)` or `view.perCaller(schema, fn)` are automatically encoded as compact binary frames with delta encoding — only changed fields are sent. A position update (3 float32 fields) is 15 bytes as a binary delta vs ~100 bytes as JSON.

See [Binary State Sync](https://actorkit.dev/concepts/binary-sync/) for the full wire protocol, frame format, and reconnection details.

## View Computation

Views are computed after every transition. The framework:
1. Calls your view function with the current state and caller
2. Compares with the previous view for this connection
3. If changed: encodes and sends (binary delta or JSON)
4. If unchanged: skips (no frame sent)

This means views are cheap — if nothing changed for a particular caller, nothing is sent.

### Scalability Impact

The choice between `view.shared` and `view.perCaller` directly affects how many clients a single actor can serve. Shared views encode once regardless of connection count; per-caller views encode once per client. See [Scalability](https://actorkit.dev/concepts/scalability/) for fan-out patterns, partitioning strategies, and practical limits.

## Discriminated Union Views (`LinkedView`)

Every view push (to both WebSocket clients and linked actors) includes a `role` field. This produces a TypeScript discriminated union:

```typescript
views: {
  admin:     view.shared(AdminView,     (state) => ({ players: state.players, settings: state.settings })),
  player:    view.perCaller(PlayerView,    (state, caller) => ({ players: state.players, myScore: state.scores[caller] })),
  spectator: view.shared(SpectatorView, (state) => ({ players: state.players })),
}

// LinkedView<GameContract> — auto-derived from the contract:
// | { role: "admin";     players: Player[]; settings: Settings }
// | { role: "player";    players: Player[]; myScore: number }
// | { role: "spectator"; players: Player[] }
```

Use `view.role` to narrow in TypeScript:

```typescript
switch (view.role) {
  case "admin":     /* view.settings is available */ break;
  case "player":    /* view.myScore is available */ break;
  case "spectator": /* only view.players */ break;
}
```

Fields common to all variants (like `players` above) are accessible without narrowing.

### In React

```tsx
// Route by role
const role = useRole();  // "admin" | "player" | "spectator" | undefined

// Select common fields — no narrowing needed
const players = useSelector((view) => view?.players);

// Select role-specific fields — pass role to narrow
const revenue = useSelector("admin", (view) => view.revenue);
// type: number | undefined (undefined if role isn't "admin")
```

### In actor-to-actor links

Same pattern. `onUpdate` receives the discriminated union:

```typescript
links: {
  game: link(GameContract, {
    onUpdate: (state, view, gameId) => {
      // view.players works without narrowing (common field)
      // view.role discriminates for role-specific fields
      return { ...state, games: { ...state.games, [gameId]: view } };
    },
  }),
},
```
