See [Actor-to-Actor Communication](https://actorkit.dev/recipes/actor-to-actor/) for the full `link()` API.

## Role Composition

Roles don't "inherit" from each other — there's no role hierarchy in the framework. Instead, compose views by extracting shared projection logic into plain functions and spreading into each role's view.

```typescript
// Extract shared projection for reuse across roles
const baseProjection = (state: GameState) => ({
  players: state.players,
  status: state.status,
  roundNumber: state.roundNumber,
});

views: {
  admin: view.shared(AdminView, (state) => ({
    ...baseProjection(state),
    revenue: state.revenue,
    settings: state.settings,
    reports: state.reports,
  })),
  moderator: view.shared(ModView, (state) => ({
    ...baseProjection(state),
    reports: state.reports,
  })),
  player: view.perCaller(PlayerView, (state, caller) => ({
    ...baseProjection(state),
    myScore: state.scores[caller],
  })),
  spectator: view.shared(SpectatorView, (state) => baseProjection(state)),
}
```

A few things to note:

- **Shared functions, not framework magic.** `baseProjection` is a plain function you write. The framework doesn't know about it — it just calls your view function.
- **Admin is a superset of spectator.** That's a consequence of spreading the same base and adding fields. TypeScript's structural typing means fields common to all views (like `players`, `status`, `roundNumber`) are accessible without narrowing on the discriminated union.
- **Each role still has its own schema.** `AdminView` and `SpectatorView` are separate `schema()` definitions with different binary layouts. The shared projection is a convenience for the _function_, not the _encoding_.
- **Keep projections pure.** View functions run after every transition. Avoid allocations or computation that scales with connection count — the framework already handles per-connection diffing.

## Related

- [Binary State Sync](https://actorkit.dev/concepts/binary-sync/) — deep dive into the binary wire protocol, delta encoding, and frame format
- [Actor-to-Actor Communication](https://actorkit.dev/recipes/actor-to-actor/) — links, services, and DO stubs for actor sync

# Binary State Sync

Source: https://actorkit.dev/concepts/binary-sync/

Actor Kit synchronizes state to connected clients over WebSocket using a binary protocol. Each client receives a role-scoped view of the actor's state, encoded directly from the schema definition into a compact binary frame. When state changes, only the fields that actually changed are sent.

## How it works

Every actor defines views per role using `schema()` and `view.shared()` / `view.perCaller()`:

```typescript
import { schema, view, uint32, float32, string, boolean, array } from "@actor-kit/core";

const PlayerView = schema({
  x: float32,
  y: float32,
  health: uint32,
  name: string,
  alive: boolean,
});

// In the actor definition:
views: {
  player: view.perCaller(PlayerView, (state, caller) => ({
    x: state.positions[caller].x,
    y: state.positions[caller].y,
    health: state.players[caller].health,
    name: state.players[caller].name,
    alive: state.players[caller].alive,
  })),
}
```

The schema serves double duty: it provides TypeScript type inference at compile time, and it defines the exact binary layout at runtime. Every field has a known size and encoding, so serialization is a single pass with no parsing ambiguity.

## The sync cycle

After every state transition, the actor broadcasts views to all connected clients:

1. **Project** — For each WebSocket, resolve the caller's role and compute their view
2. **Compare** — Check if the view changed since the last frame sent to this connection
3. **Encode** — If changed, encode as a binary delta (or full snapshot on first connect)
4. **Send** — Transmit the binary frame over WebSocket

Each connection tracks its own previous view. This means different clients can receive different deltas at different times, and a state change that doesn't affect a particular caller's view produces no frame at all.

## Snapshots and deltas

There are two frame types for state sync:

**Snapshot** — the complete view, binary-encoded. Sent on:
- First connection
- Reconnection when the client's last-known state is stale
- Role changes (the view shape may differ)

**Delta** — only the fields that changed. Sent on every subsequent state transition where at least one field differs from the previous frame.

### Delta encoding

Deltas use a bitmask to indicate which fields changed, followed by the encoded values of only those fields:

```
[bitmask: ceil(fieldCount / 8) bytes] [field₀ data] [field₃ data] ...
```

For a schema with 5 fields where only field 0 and field 3 changed:

```
Bitmask:  0b00001001  (1 byte — bits 0 and 3 set)
Data:     [field₀ value] [field₃ value]
```

Fields are written in schema definition order. The decoder reads the bitmask, then reads values for only the set bits, merging them into the previous view.

### Concrete example

A player position update in a game — `x` and `y` changed, nothing else:

| Component | Bytes |
|-----------|-------|
| Frame header | 6 |
| Bitmask (5 fields) | 1 |
| `x` (float32) | 4 |
| `y` (float32) | 4 |
| **Total** | **15 bytes** |

The same update as a JSON string would be ~80-100 bytes — the field names alone (`"x"`, `"y"`, `"health"`, `"name"`, `"alive"`) consume more space than the entire binary frame.

## Frame format

Every binary frame starts with a 6-byte header:

| Offset | Size | Field | Description |
|--------|------|-------|-------------|
| 0 | 1 | version | Schema version (for migration) |
| 1 | 1 | type | Frame type (snapshot, delta, control) |
| 2 | 4 | length | Payload length (big-endian uint32) |

**Snapshot frames** add a 1-byte role index before the payload. The client uses a single `viewSchema` for decoding — if the caller's role changes and the view shape differs, the server sends a fresh snapshot.

**Delta frames** contain the bitmask + changed field values directly as the payload.

Connection lifecycle events (errors, reconnection acks, redirects) are sent as JSON messages, not binary frames.

## Type encoding

Each schema primitive has a fixed binary representation:

| Type | Encoding | Bytes |
|------|----------|-------|
| `uint8` | Unsigned 8-bit integer | 1 |
| `uint16` | Unsigned 16-bit, big-endian | 2 |
| `uint32` | Unsigned 32-bit, big-endian | 4 |
| `float32` | IEEE 754 single-precision | 4 |
| `float64` | IEEE 754 double-precision | 8 |
| `boolean` | `0x00` or `0x01` | 1 |
| `string` | Length-prefixed UTF-8 (`uint16` length + bytes) | 2 + len |
| `array(T)` | Count-prefixed (`uint16` count + elements) | 2 + sum |
| Nested `schema({...})` | Fields concatenated in definition order | sum |

All multi-byte integers use big-endian byte order. No padding, no alignment — fields are packed contiguously.

## Client decoding

The client SDK handles binary frames automatically. Pass the view schema to `actorClient()` and the decoder is wired in:

```typescript
import { actorClient } from "@actor-kit/client";

const GameClient = actorClient(PlayerView);  // Same schema used on server

const client = GameClient.create({
  url: `wss://${location.host}/game/rooms/room-42?callerId=player-1`,
});

client.subscribe((view) => {
  // `view` is always the full, current state — snapshots and deltas
  // are merged transparently. You never see raw frames.
  renderPlayer(view.x, view.y, view.health);
});
```

When a delta arrives, the client applies the changed fields to its current view and notifies subscribers with the merged result. Your application code always sees a complete object — never a partial update.

## Reconnection

When a client reconnects after a brief disconnection, it sends a checksum of its last-known view. The server compares this checksum against the current view:

- **Match** — the client is already up to date. An acknowledgment is sent, no data retransmitted.
- **Mismatch** — the server sends a full snapshot to resync.

This avoids retransmitting state that hasn't changed during the disconnect window.

## Per-connection isolation

Each WebSocket connection maintains its own:

- **Role** — re-evaluated on every state change (roles are derived from state)
- **Previous view** — used to compute deltas for this specific connection
- **View deduplication** — if a state change doesn't alter this caller's projected view, no frame is sent

This means a state change that affects the `owner` view but not the `viewer` view will only produce a frame for the owner's connection.

## When binary sync is active

Binary sync is automatic when your views use `schema()`. If a view has a schema definition, the framework encodes it as binary frames. If no schema is defined (plain object views without `view.shared(schema, fn)` or `view.perCaller(schema, fn)`), the framework falls back to JSON strings.

In practice, any actor that uses `view.shared(MySchema, fn)` or `view.perCaller(MySchema, fn)` gets binary sync for free.

## When binary sync matters

Binary sync has the biggest impact when:

- **Updates are frequent** — games, collaborative editors, live dashboards
- **Views have many fields** — field names dominate JSON overhead
- **Only a few fields change per update** — delta encoding skips unchanged fields entirely
- **Bandwidth is constrained** — mobile networks, high-concurrency servers

For a simple counter actor with one `uint32` field, the difference between binary and JSON is negligible. For a game state with 20 fields updating at 60Hz, it's the difference between saturating a connection and running smoothly.

# Side Effects

Source: https://actorkit.dev/concepts/side-effects/

## The Problem

If a handler calls an external API and then the Durable Object crashes, the API was called but the state wasn't persisted. On restart, the handler reruns — calling the API again.

Async handlers inside DOs make this worse: `await` allows message interleaving (stale state bugs), `blockConcurrencyWhile` blocks all clients during network I/O, and a crash mid-fetch leaves no durable error record.

## The Solution: Services + execute()

Actors declare named **services** at the module level. Message handlers trigger them with `execute()`. The framework handles persistence, execution, and crash recovery.

```typescript
import { queue, setup } from "@actor-kit/worker";
import { z } from "zod";

const cart = setup({ env: z.object({ ANALYTICS: queue<{ event: string }>() }) });

cart.actor("cart", {
  // input, init, roles, views ...
  services: {
    fetchPrice: {
      fn: async (input: { itemId: string }, env) => {
        const res = await fetch(`https://api.store.com/prices/${input.itemId}`);
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${res.status}`);
        return res.json() as Promise<{ total: number }>;
      },
      onDone: (state, result, input) => ({
        ...state,
        prices: { ...state.prices, [input.itemId]: result.total },
        status: "loaded",
      }),
      onError: (state, error, input) => ({
        ...state,
        error: `${input.itemId}: ${error._tag}`,
        status: "failed",
      }),
    },
    trackEvent: {
      fn: async ({ event }: { event: string }, env) => {
        await env.ANALYTICS.send({ event });
      },
    },
  },
  messages: {
    FETCH_PRICE: cart.message(z.object({ itemId: z.string() }), (state: CartState, { itemId }, { execute }) => {
      execute("fetchPrice", { itemId });
      return { ...state, status: "loading" };
    }),
  },
});
```

A service has these parts:

- **`fn`** — async function that receives the input, the Worker `env` and the effect: `{ actorType, actorId, effectId, idempotencyKey, attempt, signal }`. Use any library: `fetch`, CF bindings (Queues, KV, R2), third-party SDKs.
- **`onDone`** — optional. Pure state transition that receives `(state, result, input)`. The result type is inferred from `fn`'s return type.
- **`errors`** — optional. The service's declared failures, a `z.discriminatedUnion("_tag", [...])`. See [Typed errors](#typed-errors).
- **`onError`** — optional. Pure state transition that receives `(state, error, input)`, where `error` is a typed, tagged error: one of the declared `errors`, `{ _tag: "Timeout", ms }` or `{ _tag: "Defect", message }`. It runs once, when the row fails for good.
- **`timeoutMs`** — optional. Time limit per try, default **30 000 ms**. When it runs out the runtime aborts `effect.signal` and the try fails as `{ _tag: "Timeout", ms }` (retried by default). Pass `effect.signal` to `fetch` and SDKs so the work actually stops. A long job must set a larger `timeoutMs`.
- **`retry`** — optional. `{ attempts, backoff: { baseMs, factor, maxMs, jitter }, while }`. Default: 3 tries, 1s then 5s apart, ±20% jitter; only `Timeout` and `Defect` are retried. `{ attempts: 1 }` turns retries off.

All three are declared at module level — no closures, fully serializable, crash-safe. The `input` argument is the original value passed to `execute()`, available in all three functions.

## Typed env

Declare the bindings an actor uses as a Zod object in its kit; the runtime parses the Worker env against it once, before the actor serves anything:

```typescript
import { d1, durableObject, kv, queue, r2, service, setup } from "@actor-kit/worker";

const checkout = setup({
  env: z.object({ PAYMENTS: service<PaymentsApi>(), SESSIONS: kv(), STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY: z.string().min(1) }),
});

checkout.actor("checkout", {
  // ...
});
```

- `service<T>()`, `durableObject<T>()`, `queue<T>()`, `kv()`, `r2()` and `d1()` check a binding's runtime shape (its methods) and type it; plain Zod schemas check vars and secrets.
- If the env does not parse, the actor refuses every request with a **500 naming each missing or wrong binding** (RPC calls throw the same message) and logs one structured line (`actor_kit.env.invalid`, binding names and reasons, never values). It never runs a handler against an unchecked env.
- `ctx.env` is typed `z.infer<typeof env>` everywhere, with no annotations: in `checkout.message()` / `checkout.timer()` / `checkout.in(state)` handlers, services' `fn(input, env, effect)`, `onDone`/`onError`'s `ctx.env` and lifecycle handlers' `ctx.env`. All of them see the parsed env (the declared bindings only).
- Without `env`, env stays `unknown` and handlers get the Worker env as it is.
- Tests take fakes typed against the schema and parse them the same way: `testActor(Contract, { env: fakes })`, `simulate({ env: { checkout: fakes } })` (keyed by contract name).

## Typed errors

A service fails with a value, not a string. Declare its failures as a tagged union and throw `fail(...)`:

```typescript
import { fail } from "@actor-kit/worker";

services: {
  charge: {
    errors: z.discriminatedUnion("_tag", [
      z.object({ _tag: z.literal("CardDeclined"), reason: z.string() }),
      z.object({ _tag: z.literal("RateLimited"), retryAfterMs: z.number() }),
    ]),
    fn: async (input: { cents: number }, env, effect) => {
      const res = await env.PAYMENTS.charge(input, { idempotencyKey: effect.idempotencyKey });
      if (res.status === 402) throw fail({ _tag: "CardDeclined", reason: res.reason });
      if (res.status === 429) throw fail({ _tag: "RateLimited", retryAfterMs: res.retryAfter });
      return res.body;
    },
    retry: { attempts: 5, while: (e) => e._tag === "RateLimited" || e._tag === "Timeout" },
    onError: (state, error) => {
      // error: CardDeclined | RateLimited | Timeout | Defect
      if (error._tag === "CardDeclined") return { ...state, status: "declined", reason: error.reason };
      return { ...state, status: "failed" };
    },
  },
},
```

- `fail(error)` marks a declared failure. The runtime parses it against `errors`; a value that doesn't parse becomes a `Defect`.
- Every service's error union also has three built-ins: `{ _tag: "Timeout", ms }` (the try ran out of time), `{ _tag: "Defect", message }` (anything thrown that isn't `fail(...)`, or a result its `result` schema refuses) and `{ _tag: "Evicted" }` (the actor was evicted while the try ran). Without `errors`, the union is just these three.
- **Default retry rule: the built-ins are retried, declared errors are not.** A declared error is a domain answer, not a transient fault: a declined card fails at once and `onError` runs. `retry.while(error)` overrides the rule per error (above, a rate limit is retried too).
- The journal stores the parsed error, so replay and restore deliver the same typed value to `onError`.
- Studio's Outbox shows the error's `_tag` in the Last error column. A declared error's fields are application values, redacted by `studio.redact` like payloads.

## Timeouts and cancellation

Every try runs under its service's `timeoutMs` (default 30 seconds), and every forward under its link's (`link(Contract, { onUpdate, timeoutMs })`, same default). The try gets an `AbortSignal` as `effect.signal`; it is aborted when:

- the try runs out of time (the try then fails as `{ _tag: "Timeout", ms }`, which is retried by default);
- a restore undoes the transition that declared the effect (the row becomes a dead letter);
- an operator redrives the effect while an earlier try of it is still running.

A result that arrives after its try was aborted is discarded, never applied. A forward's RPC cannot be cancelled mid-flight, but its late answer is discarded the same way. The Workers runtime gives a Durable Object no shutdown hook: tries in flight when an isolate is evicted die with it; what happens next depends on the service's delivery mode (below).

## Handles: the effect id, `ctx.cancel` and `ctx.effectId`

`ctx.execute()` returns the call's effect id. Keep it in state to cancel the call later, or to match its result:

```typescript
const checkout = setup({});

BUY: checkout.message(z.object({ cents: z.number() }), (s: S, { cents }, ctx) => ({
  ...s,
  pending: ctx.execute("charge", { cents }), // "812:0"
})),
ABANDON: checkout.message(z.object({}), (s: S, _p, ctx) => {
  if (s.pending !== null) ctx.cancel(s.pending);
  return { ...s, pending: null };
}),
```

`ctx.cancel(effectId)` (the same verb that cancels a timer by key) cancels a call that has not finished: one not yet run never runs, one in flight has its `effect.signal` aborted and its late result discarded. The row ends as `cancelled`; no callback runs. `onDone` and `onError` get the call's id as `ctx.effectId`.

## Results: schemas, size and audit facts

Declare `result` to parse what `fn` returns. Only the parsed value is journaled and passed to `onDone`, live and on replay, and `onDone`'s `result` is typed by it when the service comes from `kit.service()`:

```typescript
services: {
  charge: checkout.service({
    result: z.object({ chargeId: z.string() }),
    fn: async ({ cents }, env, effect) => {
      const res = await env.PAYMENTS.charge({ cents, idempotencyKey: effect.idempotencyKey });
      effect.record("gateway", res.gateway); // an audit fact on the result entry
      return res; // extra fields are dropped by the schema
    },
    onDone: (s: S, { chargeId }, _input, ctx) => ({ ...s, chargeId, pending: null }),
  }),
},
```

- A result that does not parse fails the try as a `Defect` that names the service and the issue.
- Every result's JSON must fit in `maxResultBytes` (default 128 KiB); a larger one fails the try as a `Defect`. Return a reference (an id or a URL) for large data.
- `effect.record(name, value)` attaches audit facts to the try's journal entry (`audit` beside `result`). Studio redacts them like any payload; replay ignores them.
- After every try the runtime logs one structured line, `{ event: "actor_kit.service.attempt", actorType, actorId, service, effectId, idempotencyKey, attempt, durationMs, ok, errorTag? }`. It never logs the input or the result.

## Delivery: at-least-once or at-most-once

- `delivery: "at-least-once"` (the default): tries are retried by the retry policy. A try cut off by an eviction counts as an attempt with error `{ _tag: "Evicted" }`, which is retried by default; when it was the last attempt, `onError` runs with it.
- `delivery: "at-most-once"`: one try only (`retry` is refused). The row is marked running before `fn` starts; if the actor wakes and finds it still running, the call's outcome is unknown, so it becomes a dead letter with the tag `OutcomeUnknown` and is never sent again. Studio's Outbox shows it; an operator checks the remote system and redrives it if the call did not happen.

Prefer at-least-once with `effect.idempotencyKey` whenever the remote API accepts one.

## Fire-and-Forget

Services without `onDone` or `onError` are fire-and-forget. The framework runs the function after commit but discards the result:

```typescript
services: {
  trackEvent: {
    fn: async ({ event }: { event: string }, env) => {
      await env.ANALYTICS.send({ event });
    },
  },
},
```

Trigger it the same way:

```typescript
ITEM_ADDED: cart.message(z.object({ itemId: z.string() }), (state: CartState, { itemId }, { execute }) => {
  execute("trackEvent", { event: "item_added" });
  return { ...state, items: [...state.items, itemId] };
}),
```

## Framework Execution Model

1. Message handler runs **synchronously** — returns new state (e.g., `{ status: "loading" }`)
2. State + outbox entry persisted **atomically**: `{ service: "fetchPrice", input: { itemId } }`
3. Framework runs `services.fetchPrice.fn(input, env)` **after commit**
4. On success: `onDone(currentState, result, input)` runs, state persisted, views broadcast
5. On a failure that is retried (by default `Timeout` and `Defect`) with tries left: the row waits as `retrying` and the Durable Object alarm runs it again after the backoff
6. On a failure that is not retried (by default a declared error), or of the last try: `onError(currentState, error, input)` runs with the typed error, state persisted, views broadcast; the row stays `failed`
7. On crash or eviction: restart, settle the interrupted try by the delivery mode (an Evicted attempt, or an OutcomeUnknown dead letter), then run what is due from the outbox (service name + input are serialized)

Outbox rows move through `pending` → `running` → `done`, `retrying` (and back to `running`), `failed` or `cancelled` (`ctx.cancel`). A `failed` row is a dead letter: it stays until an admin redrives it from Studio's Outbox panel, which moves it back to `pending` under the same effect id.

Messages sent with `ctx.forward(link, targetId, message)` go through the outbox too, with the same effect ids, statuses, alarm and redrive. Their retry policy belongs to the link: `link(Contract, { onUpdate, retry: { attempts, backoff } })`, same shape and defaults as a service. A send that throws (the target is unreachable) is retried; a target that cannot be resolved is a dead letter straight away. A target that answers, even with a refusal, counts as delivered.

Handlers never `await`. State is never stale. Crashes never lose intent.

## Guarantees

- **At-least-once delivery**: if the DO crashes after commit but before the service completes, the outbox entry survives. On restart, the framework re-runs the service from the persisted input.
- **No interleaving**: handlers are synchronous. State cannot change between read and write.
- **Idempotency is your responsibility**: at-least-once means duplicates are possible. Every execution has a deterministic **effect id**, `seq:index` (the transition's number and the effect's position in it). An effect id is unique only *within one actor*: two rooms at the same journal position both have effect `812:0`. Downstream, use **`effect.idempotencyKey`**, `${actorType}/${actorId}/${effectId}`, which is unique across the deployment and the same on every retry and redrive:

```typescript
charge: {
  fn: async (input: { orderId: string; cents: number }, env, effect) =>
    env.PAYMENTS.charge({ ...input, idempotencyKey: effect.idempotencyKey }),
  retry: { attempts: 5, backoff: { baseMs: 500, factor: 2 } },
},
```

Never use `effectId` alone as an idempotency key.

- **Forwards carry their effect**: a message sent with `ctx.forward()` is delivered at least once too. The target's handler reads the sender's effect as `ctx.delivery` (`{ actorType, actorId, effectId, idempotencyKey, attempt }`; `undefined` for messages that did not come through a forward) and can ignore a retried delivery it has already applied:

```typescript
DELIVER: inbox.message(z.object({ text: z.string() }), (state: Inbox, { text }, ctx) => {
  const key = ctx.delivery?.idempotencyKey;
  if (key !== undefined && state.seen.includes(key)) return state;
  return { ...state, seen: key === undefined ? state.seen : [...state.seen, key], texts: [...state.texts, text] };
}),
```

`ctx.delivery` is journaled with the event, so replay hands the same value back.

## Everything Goes Through execute()

`execute()` is the single verb for all async work:

- **Need a result?** Add `onDone` and `onError` to the service.
- **Fire-and-forget?** Skip them.
- **Need a Queue?** The service `fn` calls `env.QUEUE.send()`.
- **Need KV, R2, or D1?** The service `fn` uses env bindings directly.

## Related

- [Testing Side Effects](https://actorkit.dev/recipes/testing-side-effects/) — how to capture and assert `execute()` calls in tests

# Timers

Source: https://actorkit.dev/concepts/timers/

Actors schedule work for later with **timers** (ADR-015). A timer is declared once, scheduled from any handler with `ctx.schedule`, and fired by the Durable Object's alarm, even if the actor was evicted, hibernating or redeployed in between.

## Declaring timers

```typescript
import { setup } from "@actor-kit/worker";
import { z } from "zod";

type QuizState = { round: number; phase: string };

const quiz = setup({});

quiz.actor("quiz", {
  // input, init, roles, views ...
  messages: {
    START_ROUND: quiz.message(z.object({}), (s: QuizState, _p, ctx) => {
      const round = s.round + 1;
      ctx.schedule("roundEnd", { in: "30s", key: `round-${round}`, payload: { round } });
      return { ...s, round, phase: "answering" };
    }),
    SKIP: quiz.message(z.object({}), (s: QuizState, _p, ctx) => {
      ctx.cancel(`round-${s.round}`);
      return { ...s, phase: "reveal" };
    }),
  },
  timers: {
    roundEnd: quiz.timer(z.object({ round: z.number() }), (s: QuizState, { round }) =>
      s.round === round ? { ...s, phase: "reveal" } : s,
    ),
  },
});
```

- **`quiz.timer(schema, handler)`** (the kit's `timer`): the payload schema and a synchronous handler `(state, payload, ctx) => state`. The handler gets `ctx.key`, `ctx.lateBy`, `ctx.now()/id()/random()`, `env`, and `execute`, `forward`, `schedule`, `cancel`. A timer has no caller and no role.
- **`ctx.schedule(name, { in | at, key?, payload? })`**: available in message, lifecycle and timer handlers. `in` is milliseconds or `"500ms"`, `"30s"`, `"5m"`, `"2h"`, `"1d"`, counted from `ctx.now()`; `at` is an absolute time. Exactly one of them. The name must be declared and the payload must parse, or the handler throws and the transition is rejected.
- **`key`** is unique per actor: scheduling an existing key replaces that timer (debounce). Without a key, the timer's effect id is its key.
- **`ctx.cancel(key)`** removes a pending timer; cancelling a key that is not pending does nothing. Schedules and cancels apply in the order the handler made them.

## How they fire

- The schedule is written in the same transaction as the state change, into a `timers` table, with its absolute deadline. A transition that is rolled back schedules nothing.
- The actor keeps one Durable Object alarm at the earliest deadline (shared with outbox retries).
- When the alarm runs, every due timer fires, **late ones included**, in deadline order (ties in the order they were scheduled), each in its own transaction with its own journal event (`cause_type = "timer"`). `ctx.lateBy` says how late it fired; every timer fired by one alarm sees the same `ctx.now()`.
- Timers that a firing schedules wait for the next alarm, so a timer that reschedules itself with `in: 0` fires once per alarm, not in a loop.
- A timer whose payload no longer parses (its schema changed in a deploy) or whose transition fails is dropped and logged as an `actor_kit.timer.failed` event.
- Timers work with `journal: false`: the table is the truth.

## Studio

The **Timers** tab lists pending timers (name, key, due in, payload, with `studio.redact` applied). Admins (Studio's `mutate` scope) can **Fire now**, which runs the timer exactly as the alarm would.

## Testing

`testActor()` records `ctx.schedule` and `ctx.cancel` calls in `schedules` and `cancels` without running timers; scheduling a timer the actor does not declare throws, as in the runtime. To run timers on a virtual clock, use `simulate()`.

# Domain events

Source: https://actorkit.dev/concepts/domain-events/

The journal records every accepted message. **Domain events** record what the actor decided it
means (ADR-017): `BidPlaced`, or `BidIgnored` for a bid that changed nothing.

## Declaring and emitting

```typescript
import { setup } from "@actor-kit/worker";
import { z } from "zod";

const auction = setup({
  events: {
    BidPlaced: z.object({ bidder: z.string(), amount: z.number() }),
    BidIgnored: z.object({ bidder: z.string(), amount: z.number(), reason: z.literal("too_low") }),
  },
});

export const Auction = auction.actor("auction", {
  // ...input, init, roles, views
  messages: {
    BID: auction.message(z.object({ amount: z.number() }), (s: State, { amount }, ctx) => {
      if (amount <= highest(s)) {
        ctx.emit("BidIgnored", { bidder: ctx.caller, amount, reason: "too_low" });
        return s;
      }
      ctx.emit("BidPlaced", { bidder: ctx.caller, amount });
      return { ...s, bids: [...s.bids, { bidder: ctx.caller, amount }] };
    }),
  },
});
```

- `setup({ events })` gives `message()` and `timer()` helpers whose `ctx.emit` is typed by the
  declared events: an unknown name or a wrong payload is a type error. `auction.actor()` takes the
  events from the kit, so the definition does not repeat them.
- The payload is parsed by the event's schema when emitted. An undeclared event or an invalid
  payload fails the transition.
- Emitted events are stored on the journal row of the transition that emitted them (`emitted`).
  A transition that changes nothing but emits is still journaled.

## Testing

- `testActor(contract).send(...)` returns `emitted`.
- `simulate()` exposes `sim.events()`: every actor's events, in commit order, with the seq.
- `replayJournal()` checks that replay emits the same events, in order, and throws
  `JournalEmittedDivergenceError` at the first difference, so it also catches handler drift.

## Studio

The timeline lists each entry's emitted events (payloads redacted like message payloads).

## Publishing to a queue

```typescript
import { queue, setup } from "@actor-kit/worker";

const auction = setup({
  env: z.object({ AUCTION_EVENTS: queue() }),
  events: { /* BidPlaced, AuctionClosed, ... */ },
});

auction.actor("auction", {
  publish: { queue: "AUCTION_EVENTS", events: ["BidPlaced", "AuctionClosed"] },
  // ...
});
```

```toml
# wrangler.toml
[[queues.producers]]
binding = "AUCTION_EVENTS"
queue = "auction-events"
```

Each emitted event named in `publish.events` (a type error if it is not declared in the kit's
`events`; with an `env`, `publish.queue` must be one of its bindings)
gets an outbox row under its effect id, in the same transaction as the state, and is sent to the
Queue binding after commit, with the outbox's retries, dead letters and redrive. Studio's Outbox
panel lists the rows under the service `__publish`. The message body:

```typescript
{ actorType, actorId, seq, index, name, payload, at, causationId, correlationId, idempotencyKey }
```

`idempotencyKey` is `${actorType}/${actorId}/${seq}:${index}` and is stable across retries:
consumers dedupe on it. `simulate()` delivers published messages at once and lists them with
`sim.published("AUCTION_EVENTS")`.

# States

Source: https://actorkit.dev/concepts/states/

An actor may declare `states` (ADR-017). Data that only matters in one phase lives in that phase's
**local**, and timers scheduled with `scope: "state"` are cancelled when the actor leaves it.

```typescript
import { setup } from "@actor-kit/worker";
import { z } from "zod";

type Shared = { scores: Record<string, number> };

const quiz = setup({
  states: {
    lobby: {},
    round: { local: z.object({ n: z.number(), answers: z.record(z.string(), z.string()) }), input: z.object({ n: z.number() }) },
    reveal: {},
  },
});
const lobby = quiz.in("lobby");
const round = quiz.in("round");

export const Quiz = quiz.actor("quiz", {
  input: z.object({}),
  init: (): Shared => ({ scores: {} }),
  roles: { any: () => true },
  initial: "lobby",
  states: {
    lobby: lobby.state({
      messages: { START: lobby.message(z.object({}), (s: Shared, _p, ctx) => ctx.goto("round", s, { n: 1 })) },
    }),
    round: round.state({
      enter: (_s: Shared, { n }, ctx) => {
        ctx.schedule("roundEnd", { in: "30s", scope: "state" });
        return { n, answers: {} };
      },
      messages: {
        ANSWER: round.message(z.object({ text: z.string() }), (s: Shared, { text }, ctx) =>
          ctx.stay(s, { ...ctx.local, answers: { ...ctx.local.answers, [ctx.caller]: text } })),
      },
      timers: { roundEnd: round.timer(z.object({}).optional(), (s: Shared, _p, ctx) => ctx.goto("reveal", s)) },
    }),
    reveal: quiz.in("reveal").state({}),
  },
  views: {},
});
```

- The states are declared once, in `setup({ states })`: each one's optional `local` and `enter`
  `input` schemas. `quiz.actor()` takes them from the kit, so `initial` must name a declared state
  and `states` must define every one (each with `quiz.in(name).state({ ... })`), or it is a type error.
- The persisted state is `{ shared, phase, local, stateTimers }`. Views and roles get it
  (`PhasedStateOf<typeof quiz, Shared>`, narrowed by `phase`).
- A handler returns `ctx.stay(shared, local?)`, `ctx.goto(phase, shared, input?)`, or `shared`
  (stay, same local). `goto` checks the target and its `enter` input; `ctx.local` is typed per
  state; the local is parsed by its schema.
- Exit drops the local and cancels the phase's `scope: "state"` timers; `enter` builds the next
  local and may schedule, execute and emit.
- **`goto` to the state the actor is already in re-enters it**: exit runs (its `scope: "state"` timers
  are cancelled, its local dropped) and `enter` runs again with the new input. Say it on purpose with
  `ctx.reenter(shared, input?)` (for example to re-arm a window's timer); to keep the local and the
  timers, return `ctx.stay(...)` instead.
- A message is accepted only in the states that declare it, plus the top-level `messages`;
  otherwise it is rejected with `wrong_state`, before its guard. A message is accepted from every role
  unless it names `roles` (then other roles get `wrong_role`).
- Studio's State panel shows the phase and local; the timeline marks phase changes.

See `examples/quiz/quiz.ts` for a full contract and `tests/unit/states.test.ts` for the
behaviour under `simulate()`.

# Testing

Source: https://actorkit.dev/concepts/testing/

## Testing strategy

Actor Kit is designed for the [testing trophy](https://kentcdodds.com/blog/write-tests) — invest most in the middle layers where you get the highest confidence per test.

```
             ╱╲
            ╱  ╲           E2E (Playwright)
         ╱──────╲
        ╱          ╲
       ╱            ╲      Actor tests (testActor)
      ╱              ╲     + Integration (vitest-pool-workers)
       ╲            ╱
        ╲──────────╱
         ╲        ╱        Unit (pure functions)
          ╲──────╱
     ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━     Static analysis (TypeScript + Biome)
```

The widest part is the middle: actor tests and integration tests give you the most confidence that your actor behaves correctly. Unit tests cover pure helpers. E2E proves the full stack works in a browser.

Static analysis is the foundation — TypeScript strict mode and Biome catch entire categories of bugs before any test runs.

## Four test levels

### 1. Static analysis

TypeScript strict mode (no `any`, no `as` casts) and Biome linting. These run on every save and in pre-commit hooks.

```bash
pnpm typecheck   # strict TypeScript, zero errors
pnpm lint         # Biome: formatting, import ordering, no-explicit-any
```

### 2. Unit tests

Pure function tests with Vitest. No Actor Kit APIs, no Cloudflare runtime — just input/output.

```typescript
import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";
import { encode, decode } from "@actor-kit/core";
import { PlayerView } from "./schemas";

describe("binary encoding", () => {
  it("round-trips a player view", () => {
    const data = { x: 1.5, y: 2.5, health: 100, name: "alice", alive: true };
    const bytes = encode(PlayerView, data);
    const decoded = decode(PlayerView, bytes);
    expect(decoded).toEqual(data);
  });
});
```

Good for: schema encoding/decoding, JWT helpers, pure utility functions.

### 3. Actor tests with `testActor()`

`testActor()` is the workhorse of Actor Kit testing. It runs your full actor definition — role evaluation, message routing, Zod validation, guards, view projection, and side effect capture — without a Cloudflare runtime.

```typescript
import { testActor } from "@actor-kit/test";
import { CounterContract } from "./counter.contract";

const t = testActor(CounterContract);
```

`testActor()` accepts a contract (from `kit.actor()`) — types for `init()`, `send()`, `view()`, and `role()` are all inferred from the contract.

**Initialize state** from input:

```typescript
const state = t.init({});
```

**Send messages** and get back the result (state + captured effects):

```typescript
const { state: next } = await t.send(state, "alice", { type: "INCREMENT" });
```

**Check which role** a caller resolves to:

```typescript
expect(t.role(state, "alice")).toBe("user");
```

**Compute a view** for a caller and verify the projection:

```typescript
const { role, data } = t.view(state, "alice");
expect(role).toBe("user");
expect(data.count).toBe(0);
```

**Refused messages throw** a `RefusalError` (from `@actor-kit/core`) carrying the refusal's `code` (`unknown_message`, `invalid_payload`, `guard_failed`, `wrong_state`, `no_role`) and the whole value as `.refusal`:

```typescript
import { RefusalError } from "@actor-kit/core";

await expect(t.send(state, "alice", { type: "RESET" })).rejects.toThrow(RefusalError);
await expect(t.send(state, "alice", { type: "RESET" })).rejects.toMatchObject({ code: "guard_failed" });
```

Actors with states work the same way: `init()` returns the persisted state `{ shared, phase, local, stateTimers }`, and `send()` moves between phases as the runtime does.

**Capture service calls** without executing them:

```typescript
const { state: next, executions } = await t.send(
  state, "alice", { type: "NOTIFY_MEMBERS" }
);

expect(executions).toContainEqual(
  expect.objectContaining({ service: "notifications" })
);
```

Actor tests are fast (pure TypeScript, no I/O) and cover the most important behavior: does this message, from this caller, in this state, produce the right result?

### 4. Integration tests with `vitest-pool-workers`

Real Durable Objects, real SQLite, real WebSocket — running in the Cloudflare Workers test runtime.

**Spawn and query an actor:**

```typescript
import { env } from "cloudflare:test";

const id = env.COUNTER.idFromName("test-1");
const stub = env.COUNTER.get(id);

await stub.spawn({ actorId: "test-1", caller: "u1", callerType: "user", input: {} });
const result = await stub.send("u1", "user", { type: "INCREMENT", amount: 5 });
// { ok: true }, or a refusal: { ok: false, code, message, expected?, details?, docs }

const snapshot = await stub.getSnapshot("u1", "user");
expect(snapshot.snapshot.count).toBe(5);
```

Good for: persistence across restarts, WebSocket lifecycle, binary frame encoding over the wire, DO Alarms, outbox drain and side effect delivery.

### 5. E2E tests with Playwright

Real browser, real Worker, real Durable Object. Proves the full stack works end-to-end.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("increment button increases count", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/?id=test-" + Date.now());
  await expect(page.locator("#status")).toContainText("Connected", { timeout: 5000 });

  await page.locator("#increment").click();
  await expect(page.locator("#count")).toHaveText("1", { timeout: 3000 });
});
```

```typescript
test("two browsers see the same counter", async ({ browser }) => {
  const ctx1 = await browser.newContext();
  const ctx2 = await browser.newContext();
  const page1 = await ctx1.newPage();
  const page2 = await ctx2.newPage();

  await page1.goto("/?id=shared");
  await page2.goto("/?id=shared");

  await page1.locator("#increment").click();
  await expect(page2.locator("#count")).toHaveText("1", { timeout: 3000 });
});
```

Good for: multi-user sync, UI rendering, full auth flow, client reconnection behavior.

## What to test where

| Concern | Unit | Actor (`testActor`) | Integration (DO) | E2E |
|---------|------|---------------------|-------------------|-----|
| Schema encoding/decoding | ✓ | | | |
| JWT helpers | ✓ | | | |
| Role evaluation | | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Message routing | | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Zod validation | | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Guards | | ✓ | ✓ | |
| View projection | | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Emission capture | | ✓ | | |
| Persistence | | | ✓ | |
| WebSocket lifecycle | | | ✓ | |
| Binary delta frames | | | ✓ | |
| DO Alarms | | | ✓ | |
| Multi-user sync | | | | ✓ |
| Browser rendering | | | | ✓ |
| Full auth flow | | | | ✓ |

## Running tests

```bash
pnpm typecheck          # static analysis
pnpm test:unit          # unit + actor tests (vitest)
pnpm test:integration   # DO integration tests (vitest-pool-workers)
pnpm test               # all of the above
```

## Related

- [Testing Side Effects](https://actorkit.dev/recipes/testing-side-effects/) — how to capture and assert `execute()` calls
- [actor-kit/test API Reference](https://actorkit.dev/api/test/) — full `testActor()` API documentation

# Scalability

Source: https://actorkit.dev/concepts/scalability/

## The Actor Model on the Edge

Each actor is a Cloudflare Durable Object — a single-threaded, persistent process with its own SQLite database. Actors scale horizontally: create more actors, not bigger ones. Cloudflare runs them close to the clients that need them.

This means scalability in actor-kit is about two things:
1. **How many clients can connect to a single actor?** (fan-out)
2. **How do you decompose a large system into multiple actors?** (partitioning)

## Fan-Out: Shared vs Per-Caller Views

The biggest factor in single-actor scalability is **how many unique encoded frames** the actor must produce per state transition.

### `view.shared` — O(1) encoding

When a view doesn't depend on who's asking, all clients in that role get byte-identical frames:

```typescript
views: {
  spectator: view.shared(SpectatorView, (state) => ({
    scores: state.scores,
    currentRound: state.round,
  })),
}
```

The actor projects once and encodes once, regardless of how many spectators are connected. 100 spectators = 1 encode. 10,000 spectators = still 1 encode.

Use `view.shared` for:
- Chat rooms (everyone sees the same messages)
- Leaderboards and scoreboards
- Auction state (current bid, time remaining)
- Game lobbies (player list, ready status)
- Any "broadcast" pattern

### `view.perCaller` — O(N) encoding

When the view depends on *who's asking*, each client gets unique data:

```typescript
views: {
  player: view.perCaller(PlayerView, (state, caller) => ({
    myHand: state.hands[caller],       // only your cards
    opponentCount: state.players.length - 1,
    trick: state.trick,
  })),
}
```

The actor runs the projection and encoder once per connected client. 4 players = 4 encodes. This is fine for small player counts — a card game table with 2-8 players is well within budget.

Use `view.perCaller` for:
- Card game hands (private per player)
- Personal dashboards within a shared context
- Any view where `caller` determines what data to include

### Mixing Both

An actor can have both shared and per-caller views for different roles:

```typescript
views: {
  player: view.perCaller(PlayerView, (state, caller) => ({
    myHand: state.hands[caller],
    trick: state.trick,
  })),
  spectator: view.shared(SpectatorView, (state) => ({
    trick: state.trick,
    handSizes: state.players.map(p => state.hands[p].length),
  })),
}
```

Here, 4 players cost 4 encodes, but 1,000 spectators still cost 1 encode. The shared view handles the fan-out; the per-caller view handles the privacy.

## Practical Limits per Actor

A single Durable Object has:
- **128 MB memory** (Cloudflare limit)
- **Single-threaded execution** — one message processed at a time
- **Hibernation** — idle actors release memory, wake on next request

Rules of thumb:
- **< 100 concurrent WebSocket connections per actor** is comfortable
- **< 1,000** works with shared views and infrequent updates
- **> 1,000** — consider partitioning (see below)

The bottleneck is usually CPU (projection + encoding per transition), not memory. Shared views make fan-out nearly free. Per-caller views make it linear.

## Partitioning: Multiple Actors

When a single actor can't handle the load or the domain is naturally partitioned, split into multiple actors.

### By identity (most common)

Each user, game, room, or document is its own actor:

```
/api/counter/game-123    → Counter DO "game-123"
/api/counter/game-456    → Counter DO "game-456"
```

This is the default pattern. Cloudflare distributes DOs across its network automatically.

### By region (fog-of-war, spatial)

For large shared worlds where each player sees a subset:

```
MapRegion_5_3  →  view.shared  →  all players near (5,3)
MapRegion_5_4  →  view.shared  →  all players near (5,4)
MapRegion_6_3  →  view.shared  →  all players near (6,3)
```

Each region is a separate actor with a shared view. Players connect to the regions they can see. When a player moves across a boundary, the client disconnects from the old region and connects to the new one. Every connection within a region gets the same encoded frame — the fan-out cache handles the rest.

This turns a per-caller problem (unique fog-of-war per player) into a shared-view problem (everyone in a region sees the same tiles).

### By concern (actor-to-actor)

Split responsibilities across actor types. A game might have:

```
GameLobby    — matchmaking, player list (shared view, high fan-out)
GameTable    — game logic, hands (per-caller view, low fan-out)
Leaderboard  — scores, rankings (shared view, high fan-out)
```

Actors communicate via `ctx.execute()` (services + outbox) or `ref()` (DO-to-DO RPC). See [Actor-to-Actor Communication](https://actorkit.dev/recipes/actor-to-actor).

## Anti-Patterns

### Don't put all users in one actor

A "global chat room" actor with 10,000 users will hit CPU limits encoding state on every message. Instead:
- Shard by room/channel (each room is its own actor)
- Use a relay actor that aggregates and fans out (see [Scaling with Relays](https://actorkit.dev/recipes/scaling-with-relays))

### Don't use per-caller views for broadcast data

If the view doesn't actually need `caller`, use `view.shared`. The type system enforces this — `view.shared` callbacks literally can't reference `caller`.

### Don't fight the single-threaded model

Actors process one message at a time. If you need parallel computation, split work across multiple actors via services. Don't try to make one actor do everything.

## Summary

| Pattern | View Type | Encoding Cost | Max Connections | Example |
|---------|-----------|--------------|-----------------|---------|
| Broadcast | `view.shared` | O(1) | ~1,000+ | Chat, leaderboard, lobby |
| Private state | `view.perCaller` | O(N) | ~50-100 | Card hands, fog-of-war |
| Mixed | Both | O(1) + O(K) | Shared: ~1,000, PerCaller: ~50 | Game table + spectators |
| Partitioned | `view.shared` per partition | O(P) where P = partitions | ~1,000 per partition | World map regions |

# Actor-to-Actor Communication

Source: https://actorkit.dev/recipes/actor-to-actor/

Actors are always separate Durable Objects. They communicate by sending messages, syncing state, or reading snapshots — never by sharing memory. There are three patterns, depending on what you need.

## Links — Sync State from Another Actor

Use `link()` when one actor needs to stay in sync with another actor's view. Links are push-based subscriptions — when the source actor's state changes, the subscriber receives the new view automatically.

### Declare links

```typescript
import { link, setup } from "@actor-kit/worker";

const player = setup({});

const PlayerContract = player.actor("player", {
  input: z.object({ profileId: z.string() }),

  links: {
    profile: link(ProfileContract, {
      onUpdate: (state, view) => ({ ...state, profile: view }),
      onError: (state, error) => ({ ...state, profileError: error.message }),
    }),
    game: link(GameContract, {
      onUpdate: (state, view, gameId) => ({
        ...state,
        games: { ...state.games, [gameId]: view },
      }),
      onUnlink: (state, gameId) => {
        const { [gameId]: _, ...rest } = state.games;
        return { ...state, games: rest };
      },
    }),
    // **Note:** `onError` and `onUnlink` callbacks are declared in the link
    // definition for future use. Currently, only `onUpdate` is invoked by the
    // runtime. Handle cleanup in your `unlink()` message handler directly.
  },

  init: (input) => ({
    profileId: input.profileId,
    profile: null as LinkedView<ProfileContract> | null,
    games: {},      // linked later via messages
  }),

  messages: {
    SETUP: player.message(z.object({}), {
      guard: (_state: PlayerState, _payload, ctx) => ctx.callerType === "service",
      handler: (state: PlayerState, _payload, { link }) => {
        link("profile", state.profileId);  // view arrives via onUpdate
        return state;
      },
    }),
    JOIN_GAME: player.message(z.object({ gameId: z.string() }), (state: PlayerState, { gameId }, { link }) => {
      link("game", gameId);   // fire-and-forget, view arrives via onUpdate
      return { ...state, gameStatus: "connecting" };
    }),
    LEAVE_GAME: player.message(z.object({ gameId: z.string() }), (state: PlayerState, { gameId }, { unlink }) => {
      unlink("game", gameId);
      return state;
    }),
  },

  views: {
    user: view.shared(PlayerView, (state: PlayerState) => ({
      profileName: state.profile?.name ?? "",
      games: Object.keys(state.games),
    })),
  },
});
```

### How it works

1. `link("profile", id)` in the `SETUP` message handler → subscribes asynchronously. The first view arrives via `onUpdate`. State starts null, becomes non-null on first update.
2. `link("game", gameId)` in a message handler → subscribes asynchronously. Same pattern — the first view arrives via `onUpdate`.
3. When the source actor's state changes → `broadcastViews()` pushes the new view to all subscribers (alongside WebSocket clients). The subscriber's `onUpdate` reducer runs, persisting the new state.
4. On crash/restart → subscriptions are re-registered. If the source changed during downtime, `onUpdate` fires with the current view.

> **Note:** Init-time link resolution (blocking fetch during init) is planned but not yet implemented. For now, use a setup message to establish links after init.

### Discriminated union views

The source actor resolves the subscriber's role on every push — same as for WebSocket clients. The view includes a `role` discriminant, producing a TypeScript discriminated union:

```typescript
// GameContract has these views:
views: {
  admin:     view.shared(AdminView, (state) => ({ players: state.players, settings: state.settings, revenue: state.revenue })),
  player:    view.perCaller(PlayerView, (state, caller) => ({ players: state.players, myScore: state.scores[caller] })),
  spectator: view.shared(SpectatorView, (state) => ({ players: state.players })),
}

// LinkedView<GameContract> is auto-derived:
// | { role: "admin";     players: Player[]; settings: Settings; revenue: number }
// | { role: "player";    players: Player[]; myScore: number }
// | { role: "spectator"; players: Player[] }
```

In `onUpdate`, narrow with `view.role`:

```typescript
onUpdate: (state, view, gameId) => {
  switch (view.role) {
    case "admin":
      // TS narrows: view has settings, revenue
      return { ...state, games: { ...state.games, [gameId]: view } };
    case "player":
      // TS narrows: view has myScore
      return { ...state, games: { ...state.games, [gameId]: view } };
    case "spectator":
      return { ...state, games: { ...state.games, [gameId]: view } };
  }
}
```

Fields common to all variants (like `players` above) are accessible without narrowing.

### Role changes at runtime

If the subscriber's role changes (e.g., promoted from player to admin), the next push arrives with the new role's view. The `switch` on `view.role` handles it naturally — no stale data, no data leaks.

### Collections

Call `link(name, id)` with different IDs. `onUpdate`/`onUnlink` receive the `id` as third arg:

```typescript
link("game", "game-1");   // subscribe to game-1
link("game", "game-2");   // subscribe to game-2
link("game", "game-3");   // subscribe to game-3

unlink("game", "game-2"); // unsubscribe from game-2
unlink("game");            // unsubscribe from all
```

Each target resolves the subscriber's role independently — you can be admin on game-1 and a player on game-2.

## Services — Fire-and-Forget or Async Effects

Use `execute()` with a named service when you need to call an external API, send to a Queue, or write to KV/D1/R2. The service runs asynchronously after the state change commits.

```typescript
const zone = setup({});

zone.actor("zone", {
  services: {
    transferPlayer: {
      fn: async ({ targetZone, playerId, health, inventory }, env) => {
        const stub = env.ZONE.get(env.ZONE.idFromName(targetZone));
        const result = await stub.send("system", "service", {
          type: "PLAYER_ARRIVED",
          playerId, health, inventory,
        });
        // send() resolves to { ok: true } or a refusal { ok: false, code, message, ... }
        if (!result.ok) throw new Error(result.message);
      },
      onDone: (state, result, input) => ({
        ...state,
        transferStatus: "confirmed",
      }),
      onError: (state, error, input) => ({
        ...state,
        transferStatus: "failed",
        error: error._tag,
      }),
    },
  },

  messages: {
    TRANSFER_PLAYER: zone.message(
      z.object({ playerId: z.string(), targetZone: z.string() }),
      (state: ZoneState, { playerId, targetZone }, { execute }) => {
        execute("transferPlayer", {
          targetZone,
          playerId,
          health: state.players[playerId].health,
          inventory: state.players[playerId].inventory,
        });
        const { [playerId]: _, ...remaining } = state.players;
        return { ...state, players: remaining, transferStatus: "pending" };
      },
    ),
  },
});
```

Services are durable — the outbox persists the service name and input atomically with the state change. If the DO crashes, pending services retry on restart.

## Direct RPC with Typed DO Stubs

Use Cloudflare's native typed DO bindings inside your Worker's `fetch` handler (not inside an actor) when you need to interact with actors from request-handling code — spawning, sending messages, or reading snapshots.

Run `npx wrangler types` to generate typed bindings for your `Env`. This gives you `DurableObjectNamespace<ZoneActor>` on `env.ZONE`, with full type safety for `spawn()`, `send()`, and `getSnapshot()`.

```typescript
import type { ZoneActor } from "./zone";

export default {
  async fetch(request: Request, env: Env) {
    const stub = env.ZONE.get(env.ZONE.idFromName("forest-north"));

    await stub.spawn({
      actorId: "forest-north",
      caller: "system",
      callerType: "service",
      input: { biome: "forest" },
    });

    const sent = await stub.send("system", "service", {
      type: "SPAWN_NPC",
      npcType: "merchant",
    });
    if (!sent.ok) return Response.json(sent, { status: 409 }); // a Refusal: code, message, docs

    const { snapshot, role } = await stub.getSnapshot("system", "service");
    return Response.json(snapshot);
  },
};
```

## Which to Use

| Pattern | When | Response? | Delivery | Stays in sync? |
|---------|------|-----------|----------|---------------|
| `link()` | Actor needs another actor's state | Push-based view updates | Durable (outbox + subscription) | Yes |
| `execute()` + service | Actor needs to call an API or notify another actor | `onDone`/`onError` | At-least-once via outbox | No — one-shot |
| DO stub (`env.BINDING.get(...)`) | Worker fetch handler | Direct RPC return | Immediate | No |

**Links** are for ongoing state sync between actors — Player staying in sync with Profile, Game syncing player profiles.

**Services** are for one-shot async effects — calling an API, sending to a Queue, or firing a notification to another actor without staying subscribed.

**DO stubs** are for request-handling code outside actors — spawning actors, sending messages, reading snapshots from a Worker route handler.

## Actor Discovery via `ctx.exports`

When all actors deploy in a single Worker (the recommended pattern), Cloudflare's `ctx.exports` provides automatic namespace discovery — no manual env bindings needed between actors.

### Enable the compat flag

```jsonc
// wrangler.jsonc
{
  "compatibility_flags": ["enable_ctx_exports"]
}
```

### How it works

`createActorClass()` stamps each DO class with its contract name. The framework's `resolveNamespace()` iterates `ctx.exports` to find the matching class:

```typescript
import { createRef } from "@actor-kit/worker";

// Inside a message handler (ctx.exports is NOT available on message ctx):
const ref = createRef(ProfileContract, env, profileId);
await ref.send("system", "service", { type: "UPDATE_NAME", name: "Alice" }); // { ok: true } or a Refusal
```

> **Note:** `ctx.exports`-based resolution happens automatically inside the framework's `link()` and `resolveNamespace()` internals. Message handlers do not have access to `ctx.exports` — use the `createRef(contract, env, actorId)` overload which looks up the env binding directly.

The `createRef(contract, exports, env, actorId)` overload (used internally by the framework):
1. Searches `exports` for a DO class whose contract name matches
2. Falls back to `env.BINDING_NAME` if not found in exports
3. Throws if not found in either

### Fallback: env bindings

For multi-Worker deployments or when `ctx.exports` isn't available, env bindings still work:

```typescript
// Legacy: env binding lookup
const ref = createRef(ProfileContract, env, profileId);
```

You can also use `resolveNamespace()` directly:

```typescript
import { resolveNamespace } from "@actor-kit/worker";

const namespace = resolveNamespace("profile", ctx.exports, env);
```

## Wrangler Bindings

All actors must be declared as Durable Object classes in your `wrangler.jsonc` (required for storage migrations). With `ctx.exports` enabled, the `bindings` array is only needed for cross-Worker actors:

```json
{
  "durable_objects": {
    "bindings": [
      { "name": "ZONE", "class_name": "ZoneActor" },
      { "name": "PLAYER", "class_name": "PlayerActor" },
      { "name": "PROFILE", "class_name": "ProfileActor" }
    ]
  }
}
```

The binding name (e.g., `"ZONE"`) is derived from the actor's contract name: `zone.actor("zone", ...)` → binding `ZONE`. It must match the key in your Worker's `Env` type.

## Related

- [Side Effects](https://actorkit.dev/concepts/side-effects/) — how `execute()` and the transactional outbox work
- [Views](https://actorkit.dev/concepts/views/) — per-role view projections and discriminated union types
- [Testing Side Effects](https://actorkit.dev/recipes/testing-side-effects/) — how to capture and assert `execute()` calls and link subscriptions in tests

# Scaling with Relays

Source: https://actorkit.dev/recipes/scaling-with-relays/

A single Durable Object can handle hundreds of WebSocket connections comfortably, but not hundreds of thousands. Every state change calls `broadcastViews()`, which encodes and sends a frame to every connected client — O(N) per transition. At scale, this becomes the bottleneck.

Relay actors solve this by splitting fan-out across multiple DOs.

## The Pattern

```
Source DO (1) ──link──> Relay DOs (100) ──WebSocket──> Clients (100K)
```

The source actor holds all state and runs all transitions. Relay actors subscribe to the source via `link()` and forward views to their own WebSocket clients. The source broadcasts to ~100 relays instead of 100,000 clients. Each relay broadcasts to ~1,000 clients.

## Source Actor

The source actor doesn't change. It defines state, messages, and views as usual. Relay DOs appear as linked subscribers — the source treats them the same as any other subscriber.

```typescript
const game = setup({});

const GameContract = game.actor("game", {
  // ... normal actor definition
  roles: {
    service: (state, caller, { callerType }) => callerType === "service",
    admin: (state, caller) => state.adminId === caller,
    player: (state, caller) => state.playerIds.includes(caller),
    spectator: () => true,
  },
  views: {
    service: view.shared(ServiceView, (state) => ({
      players: state.players,
      settings: state.settings,
      scores: state.scores,
      status: state.status,
    })),
    admin: view.shared(AdminView, (state) => ({ /* ... */ })),
    player: view.shared(PlayerView, (state) => ({ /* ... */ })),
    spectator: view.shared(SpectatorView, (state) => ({ /* ... */ })),
  },
});
```

The `service` role returns a superset view — all the data any client role might need. Relays connect as services.

## Relay Actor

The relay links to the source actor and passes through views to its own clients.

```typescript
const relay = setup({});

const RelayContract = relay.actor("relay", {
  input: z.object({ sourceId: z.string() }),

  links: {
    source: link(GameContract, {
      onUpdate: (state, view) => ({ ...state, currentView: view }),
    }),
  },

  init: (input) => ({
    sourceId: input.sourceId,
    currentView: null as LinkedView<GameContract> | null,
  }),

  roles: { viewer: () => true },

  messages: {
    CONNECT_SOURCE: relay.message(z.object({}), {
      guard: (_state: RelayState, _payload, ctx) => ctx.callerType === "service",
      handler: (state: RelayState, _payload, { link }) => {
        link("source", state.sourceId);
        return state;
      },
    }),
  },

  views: {
    viewer: view.shared(GameView, (state) => state.currentView),
  },
});
```

> **Note:** Init-time link resolution (`await link()` in init) is planned but not yet implemented. For now, use a setup message (`CONNECT_SOURCE`) to establish links after init. The relay spawns, receives the message, and `onUpdate` populates the view.

## Re-projecting Per-Client Views

If clients need role-specific views, the relay can re-project from the superset view it receives from the source. The source resolves the relay as a `service` role, so the relay gets all fields. The relay then defines its own roles and projects accordingly:

```typescript
const RelayContract = relay.actor("relay", {
  input: z.object({ sourceId: z.string() }),

  links: {
    source: link(GameContract, {
      onUpdate: (state, view) => ({ ...state, currentView: view }),
    }),
  },

  init: (input) => ({
    sourceId: input.sourceId,
    currentView: null as LinkedView<GameContract> | null,
  }),

  messages: {
    CONNECT_SOURCE: relay.message(z.object({}), {
      guard: (_state: RelayState, _payload, ctx) => ctx.callerType === "service",
      handler: (state: RelayState, _payload, { link }) => {
        link("source", state.sourceId);
        return state;
      },
    }),
  },

  roles: {
    admin: (state, caller) => state.currentView?.settings.adminIds.includes(caller) ?? false,
    viewer: () => true,
  },

  views: {
    admin: view.shared(AdminView, (state) => ({
      players: state.currentView?.players ?? [],
      settings: state.currentView?.settings ?? {},
      scores: state.currentView?.scores ?? {},
      status: state.currentView?.status ?? "waiting",
    })),
    viewer: view.shared(ViewerView, (state) => ({
      players: state.currentView?.players ?? [],
      status: state.currentView?.status ?? "waiting",
    })),
  },
});
```

The relay's role resolution runs independently of the source's. The relay decides what each of _its_ clients can see.

## Client Routing

The Worker's `fetch` handler assigns clients to relays instead of connecting them directly to the source:

```typescript
export default {
  async fetch(request, env, ctx) {
    // Simple modulo routing — assign to relay based on hash
    const callerId = getCallerId(request);
    const relayIndex = hashToIndex(callerId, RELAY_COUNT);
    const relayId = `relay-${gameId}-${relayIndex}`;

    const relay = env.RELAY.get(env.RELAY.idFromName(relayId));
    // Forward WebSocket upgrade to relay instead of source
  },
};
```

Consistent hashing ensures the same client always routes to the same relay, preserving connection affinity across reconnects.

## When to Use

| Connections | Pattern |
|------------|---------|
| < 1,000 | Direct — single actor handles all clients |
| 1,000 - 100,000 | Relay — source + N relay actors |
| > 100,000 | Multiple relay tiers or external pub/sub |

Most applications never need relays. Start with direct connections and add relays when `broadcastViews()` latency becomes measurable.

## Limitations

- **Added latency.** Every view update travels source → relay → client instead of source → client. For a game running at 60Hz updates, this adds one hop of DO-to-DO RPC latency (~1-5ms intra-colo).
- **Brief staleness.** Relay views may lag behind the source by one update cycle. Clients on different relays can see slightly different snapshots at the same instant.
- **Cost.** Each relay is a separate Durable Object with its own storage and compute billing. 100 relays = 100x the DO fixed costs, though per-request costs are spread across them.
- **Messages go to the source.** Clients send messages through the relay, but the relay forwards them to the source for processing. The relay is read-only — it never mutates game state.

## Related

- [Actor-to-Actor Communication](https://actorkit.dev/recipes/actor-to-actor/) — the `link()` API that relays use to subscribe to the source
- [Views](https://actorkit.dev/concepts/views/) — per-role view projections and binary encoding

# Testing Side Effects

Source: https://actorkit.dev/recipes/testing-side-effects/

Side effects (`execute()`) are recorded during transitions but not executed in `testActor()`. This lets you assert exactly what was scheduled without hitting external services.

## Capturing executions

`send()` always returns `{ state, executions, links, unlinks, forwards }`:

```typescript
import { testActor } from "@actor-kit/test";
import { OrderContract } from "./order";

const t = testActor(OrderContract);
let state = t.init({ items: ["widget"] });

const { state: next, executions } = await t.send(
  state, "alice", { type: "PLACE_ORDER" }
);
```

`executions` contains every `execute()` call made during the transition.

## Asserting service executions

Each execution has `{ service, input }`:

```typescript
// Verify a named service was called
expect(executions).toContainEqual(
  expect.objectContaining({
    service: "ORDER_QUEUE",
    input: expect.objectContaining({ items: ["widget"] }),
  })
);

// Verify an inventory reservation
expect(executions).toContainEqual(
  expect.objectContaining({
    service: "RESERVE_ITEMS",
    input: expect.objectContaining({ warehouse: "warehouse-1" }),
  })
);
```

## Asserting no side effects

```typescript
const { executions } = await t.send(
  state, "alice", { type: "INCREMENT" }
);

expect(executions).toHaveLength(0);
```

## Asserting execution counts

```typescript
const { executions } = await t.send(
  state, "alice", { type: "NOTIFY_ALL" }
);

// Exactly 3 notifications sent
expect(executions).toHaveLength(3);

// All went to the same service
expect(executions.every(e => e.service === "NOTIFICATIONS")).toBe(true);
```

## Integration testing side effects

`testActor()` captures but doesn't run effects. To test actual delivery (outbox drain, retry behavior, actor-to-actor), use integration tests with `vitest-pool-workers`:

```typescript
import { env } from "cloudflare:test";

const id = env.ORDER.idFromName("test-order");
const stub = env.ORDER.get(id);

await stub.spawn({ actorId: "test-order", caller: "alice", callerType: "user", input: { items: ["widget"] } });
await stub.send("alice", "user", { type: "PLACE_ORDER" });

// The outbox drains asynchronously — the target actor receives the message
const inventory = env.INVENTORY.get(env.INVENTORY.idFromName("warehouse-1"));
const snapshot = await inventory.getSnapshot("system", "service");
expect(snapshot.snapshot.reserved).toContain("widget");
```

# Storybook Testing

Source: https://actorkit.dev/recipes/storybook/

`@actor-kit/storybook` provides a Storybook decorator and mock client for rendering components that depend on actor-kit state — without a real WebSocket connection.

## Install

```bash
pnpm add -D @actor-kit/storybook
```

## Static stories with `withActorKit`

The `withActorKit` decorator creates a mock client with initial view data and wraps your story in the context provider:

```typescript
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from "@storybook/react";
import { expect, within } from "@storybook/test";
import { withActorKit } from "@actor-kit/storybook";
import { Counter } from "./Counter";
import { CounterCtx } from "./counter.context";

const meta: Meta<typeof Counter> = {
  title: "Counter",
  component: Counter,
};
export default meta;
type Story = StoryObj<typeof Counter>;

export const Default: Story = {
  decorators: [
    withActorKit({
      context: CounterCtx,
      view: { count: 0, lastUpdatedBy: "" },
    }),
  ],
  play: async ({ canvasElement }) => {
    const canvas = within(canvasElement);
    await expect(canvas.getByText("0")).toBeVisible();
  },
};

export const WithCount: Story = {
  decorators: [
    withActorKit({
      context: CounterCtx,
      view: { count: 42, lastUpdatedBy: "alice" },
    }),
  ],
  play: async ({ canvasElement }) => {
    const canvas = within(canvasElement);
    await expect(canvas.getByText("42")).toBeVisible();
  },
};
```

## Interactive stories with `onSend`

Use `onSend` to handle button clicks and update the view in play functions:

```typescript
export const Interactive: Story = {
  decorators: [
    withActorKit({
      context: CounterCtx,
      view: { count: 0, lastUpdatedBy: "" },
      onSend: (message) => {
        if (message.type === "INCREMENT") {
          // Return a new view — the mock client updates and re-renders
          return { count: 1, lastUpdatedBy: "test" };
        }
      },
    }),
  ],
  play: async ({ canvasElement }) => {
    const canvas = within(canvasElement);
    await expect(canvas.getByText("0")).toBeVisible();

    // Click increment
    await canvas.getByRole("button", { name: "+" }).click();

    // View should update
    await expect(canvas.getByText("1")).toBeVisible();
  },
};
```

## Role-specific rendering

Test how your UI adapts to different roles:

```typescript
export const OwnerView: Story = {
  decorators: [
    withActorKit({
      context: TodoCtx,
      view: { todos: [{ id: "1", text: "Test", done: false }], memberCount: 2 },
      role: "owner",
    }),
  ],
  play: async ({ canvasElement }) => {
    const canvas = within(canvasElement);
    // Owner should see delete button
    await expect(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: "Delete" })).toBeVisible();
  },
};

export const ViewerView: Story = {
  decorators: [
    withActorKit({
      context: TodoCtx,
      view: { todoCount: 3, doneCount: 1 },
      role: "viewer",
    }),
  ],
  play: async ({ canvasElement }) => {
    const canvas = within(canvasElement);
    // Viewer should see counts, not individual todos
    await expect(canvas.getByText("3 todos")).toBeVisible();
  },
};
```

## Mock client directly

For more control, create a mock client directly:

```typescript
import { createMockClient } from "@actor-kit/storybook";

const client = createMockClient<CounterView, CounterMessage>({
  initialView: { count: 0, lastUpdatedBy: "" },
  role: "user",
  onSend: (message) => {
    if (message.type === "INCREMENT") {
      return { count: (client.view?.count ?? 0) + 1, lastUpdatedBy: "test" };
    }
  },
});

// Use in a custom provider setup
<CounterCtx.Provider client={client}>
  <Counter />
</CounterCtx.Provider>
```

## API

### `withActorKit(options)`

| Option | Type | Required | Description |
|--------|------|----------|-------------|
| `context` | `actorContext()` result | Yes | The context that provides `useView()`, `useSend()`, etc. |
| `view` | `TView` | Yes | Initial view data |
| `role` | `string` | No | Role for `useRole()` (default: "user") |
| `onSend` | `(message) => TView \| void` | No | Handle `send()` calls. Return a new view to update, or void to ignore. |

### `createMockClient(options)`

| Option | Type | Required | Description |
|--------|------|----------|-------------|
| `initialView` | `TView` | Yes | Initial view data |
| `role` | `string` | No | Role (default: "user") |
| `connectionState` | `ConnectionState` | No | Initial state (default: "connected") |
| `onSend` | `(message) => TView \| void` | No | Handle sends interactively |

# Studio

Source: https://actorkit.dev/studio/overview/

Actor Kit Studio is a built-in debugging tool for actor-kit. Connect to any running actor and see its state, timeline, connections, outbox, and views — all updating in real-time.

## What you can see

- **Current state** — live-updating JSON view of the actor's state
- **Timeline** — chronological log of every state mutation with its cause (message, service completion, link update, lifecycle event, timer, restore). Admins can **Restore to here** on an entry: the actor goes back to that point as a new `restore` event (history is kept, timers pending then come back, nothing that already ran runs again, and service results recorded since are delivered again).
- **Connections** — active WebSocket clients with caller identity and role
- **Timers** — pending durable timers (name, key, due in, payload); admins can fire one now
- **Outbox** — service executions by effect id, with status (pending, running, retrying, done, failed), tries, next try and last error (with its `_tag`: `Timeout`, `Defect` or a declared error). Admins can redrive a failed row.
- **Links** — actor-to-actor subscriptions (who this actor links to and who subscribes to it)
- **Views** — computed view projections per role

## How it works

Every actor automatically records a timeline of state mutations to its SQLite storage. The timeline captures:

| Cause | When |
|-------|------|
| `init` | Actor initialized for the first time |
| `message` | Client sent a message (includes payload, caller, role) |
| `lifecycle.connect` | Client WebSocket connected |
| `lifecycle.disconnect` | Client WebSocket disconnected |
| `service.onDone` | Service completed successfully |
| `service.onError` | Service failed |
| `link.onUpdate` | Linked actor pushed new state |
| `link.onError` | Link subscription failed |
| `link.onUnlink` | Link was removed |

Each entry stores the full state snapshot after the mutation, so you can scrub through the timeline and see the exact state at any point.

## Architecture

```
Studio UI  <-->  actorKitStudio() middleware  <-->  Actor DOs
                        |                              |
                        v                              v
                 StudioRegistry DO              Timeline table
                 (actor index)                  (per-actor SQLite)
```

- **StudioRegistry** — a Durable Object that tracks all known actor instances. Actors register themselves automatically.
- **Timeline table** — each actor stores its mutation history in a ring buffer (default 500 entries) in its own SQLite.
- **Studio WebSocket** — the studio connects to actors with a special `__studio` identity that bypasses role evaluation and receives live updates.

## Quick start

See the [setup guide](https://actorkit.dev/studio/setup/) for installation and configuration.

# Studio Setup

Source: https://actorkit.dev/studio/setup/

## Install

```bash
pnpm add @actor-kit/studio
```

## Configure your Worker

### 1. Export the StudioRegistry

Add the `StudioRegistry` Durable Object to your Worker's exports:

```typescript
import { actorKitStudio, StudioRegistry } from "@actor-kit/studio";

// Export the registry DO class
export { StudioRegistry };
```

### 2. Add the middleware

Insert `actorKitStudio()` at the top of your Worker's `fetch` handler. It intercepts `/__studio/*` routes and passes everything else through:

```typescript
export default {
  async fetch(request: Request, env: Env, ctx: ExecutionContext) {
    // Studio middleware — handles /__studio/* routes
    const studio = actorKitStudio(request, env, ctx);
    if (studio) return studio;

    // ... your normal routing below
  },
};
```

### 3. Add the DO binding

In your `wrangler.toml`, add a binding for the `StudioRegistry`:

```toml
[[durable_objects.bindings]]
name = "STUDIO_REGISTRY"
class_name = "StudioRegistry"

[[migrations]]
tag = "v2"  # increment your migration tag
new_sqlite_classes = ["StudioRegistry"]
```

### 4. Production: put `/__studio` behind Cloudflare Access

In local development (`wrangler dev` on `localhost` / `127.0.0.1`) with no Access settings, Studio is open. In production, Studio requires [Cloudflare Access](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/): people sign in with SSO, and each agent gets its own service token. The middleware verifies the `Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion` JWT itself (RS256, issuer, audience, expiry), so a route Access doesn't cover (e.g. `*.workers.dev`) is still refused. See ADR-014.

Set these on the Worker:

| Setting | How | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `STUDIO_ACCESS_TEAM_DOMAIN` | var | `<team>.cloudflareaccess.com` |
| `STUDIO_ACCESS_AUD` | var | AUD tag of the Studio Access application |
| `STUDIO_ADMIN_EMAILS` | `wrangler secret put` | comma-separated emails allowed to **mutate** (e.g. future journal restore) |
| `STUDIO_CALLER_HASH_KEY` | `wrangler secret put` | HMAC key that hashes callers for agents |

```bash
openssl rand -hex 32 | wrangler secret put STUDIO_CALLER_HASH_KEY
wrangler secret put STUDIO_ADMIN_EMAILS
```

## Authentication and permissions

| Who | How | Can |
|---|---|---|
| Localhost, no Access settings | nothing | read + mutate (dev) |
| Person | Access SSO cookie (browser) or `cloudflared access token` (CLI) | read; mutate if in `STUDIO_ADMIN_EMAILS` |
| Agent | Access service token (`CF-Access-Client-Id` / `-Secret`) | read only, never mutate; callers are hashed |
| Anything else | | 401 (no or invalid token) / 403 (Studio not configured) |

Every Studio request logs one `studio.request` JSON line (principal, subject, route, actor, status, duration), never bodies or tokens.

## Redaction
